title: Members of Trump's cabinet remained on decoy plane, after president's quiet exit
excerpt:
Two members of US President Donald Trump's cabinet were on a decoy plane that Trump secretly exited before boarding a different flight in Turkey last month, CBS News reports.

Secretary of State Marco...
body_text:
Two members of US President Donald Trump's cabinet were on a decoy plane that Trump secretly exited before boarding a different flight in Turkey last month, CBS News reports.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remained aboard what was believed to be Air Force One and didn't join a flight that was provided to Trump over security concerns involving Iran.

After Trump entered Air Force One on 8 July with both officials and members of the press, he hid on a catering truck to be clandestinely transported to a military plane.

The label "Air Force One" applies to any plane the president is on, but in this case the original craft kept the call signal, becoming a decoy.

According to CBS - the BBC's US partner - Rubio and Bessent remained on board the first aircraft to maintain the line of succession in the event something happened to Trump

In the event that the president dies or is incapacitated, Vice-President JD Vance would take power, followed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the President Pro Tempore of the Senate.

The Secretary of State comes next in line, followed by the treasury secretary.

Others who stayed on the initial aircraft designated as Air Force One included White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Steven Cheung, the White House's communications director.

The second aircraft that flew President Trump out of Ankara also included Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, according to US media reports.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Speaking to reporters on Monday night, Trump said the decision to undertake the deception was made by the US military and the Secret Service, who "wanted me to go in a different flight".

The nature of the security threat remains unclear, with Trump providing no specifics, saying only that he gets "a lot of threats".

"Any consequential president has a lot of threats," he added.

It is also unclear what the cabinet secretaries and other officials knew of the operation. Members of the press have said they were not aware that they were on a decoy flight.

Various ruses, often referred to as "shell games" by Secret Service personnel, are common.

Identical versions of the president's heavily armoured limousine, for example, often switch positions in motorcades, as do helicopters transporting the president in the air.

More elaborate operations often take place during high-risk trips abroad, afnd in those cases reporters on Air Force One are typically briefed and asked not to report the movements in real-time.

In March 2000, for example, then-President Bill Clinton flew to the Pakistani capital of Islamabad on an unmarked executive jet that landed after a decoy jet with the livery of Air Force One.

Ahead of the trip, the White House informed USA Today reporter Susan Page - then the head of the White House Correspondent's Association - of the security arrangements.

"They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken because of the dangers flying there, including the use of the decoy plane," Page revealed for the first time this week.

"Of course, the dangers threatened the journalists covering the trip as well as President Clinton," she said in an interview with the Washington Post.

It is not currently clear what, if any, danger the occupants of the plane carrying Rubio, Bessent, other staff and the White House press pool were in during the Ankara trip.

The White House Correspondent's Association has not publicly commented on the incident.

Decoys to hide presidents are common - but elaborate Trump ruse was different level

Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump?

title: John Hinckley Jr gives his thoughts on Jodie Foster 45 years after shooting Ronald Reagan to impress her
excerpt:
Jodie Foster spoke to Fox News Digital about being honored at hand and foot ceremony on Friday.

John Hinckley Jr., the man who shot former President Ronald Reagan in 1981 to impress Jodie Foster, sai...
body_text:
Jodie Foster spoke to Fox News Digital about being honored at hand and foot ceremony on Friday.

John Hinckley Jr., the man who shot former President Ronald Reagan in 1981 to impress Jodie Foster, said he wants nothing but good things for the actress.

"I just wish Jodie Foster well," he said. "I don’t really see her movies, but I wish her well, and I know she’s doing quite well. And that’s all I can say: I just, I wish Jodie well, and I hope she has a good life."

The 71-year-old explained on the "Mark Joesph Show" in an exclusive preview shared with Entertainment Weekly that when he shot Reagan 45 years ago in a delusional state, he believed he would spend the rest of his life with the "Silence of the Lambs" actress.

REAGAN SHOOTER CALLS LINK TO WASHINGTON HOTEL ‘SPOOKY’ AFTER ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT AT SAME SITE

John Hinckley Jr., seen left in his 1981 mugshot, spoke about Jodie Foster in a new interview. (Bureau of Prisons/Getty Images; Jamie McCarthy/WireImage)

"I wanted to have like this union with Jodie Foster, and live the rest of my life with her and all these things that, of course, were delusional, but I was believing those things at that time, so the best outcome would have been to just have like this union with Jodie Foster," Hinckley told Joseph after the host asked what he believed at the time would be the best thing that could come out of the shooting.

John Hinckley Jr. said he wishes Jodie Foster well. (Getty Images)

He explained that he honestly believed at the time that Foster would "join me wherever I was. You know, I didn’t know if I was going to be in jail or hospital or what, but after things settled down, I had this notion that she was going to join me wherever I was."

It came out shortly after Hinckley’s assassination attempt that left Reagan with a broken rib, punctured lung and internal bleeding, that he was obsessed with Foster after seeing her in "Taxi Driver," and thought the shooting would make her notice him.

JODIE FOSTER HAUNTED BY HORRIFIC DOG TRAGEDY, BELIEVES SHE GAVE UP WHAT SHE LOVES MOST FOR SUCCESS

John Hinckley Jr. stands for a portrait in Williamsburg, Virginia, in 2022. (AFP via Getty Images)

Hinckley was found not guilty by reason of insanity after shooting the former president outside the Washington Hilton two months after he was elected.

Former White House Press Secretary James Brady was shot in the head and suffered brain damage and partial paralysis, which helped lead to his death in 2014. His death was ruled a homicide.

Two other men were also wounded in the shooting.

Hinckley was committed to a psychiatric hospital after the trial and released in 2016. By 2022, he was living in Virginia without any court restrictions.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

President Ronald Reagan waves to the crowd outside the Hilton Hotel in Washington, D.C., just before an assassination attempt on March 30, 1981. (CONSOLIDATED NEWS PICTURES/AFP via Getty Images)

Hinckley admitted to Joseph, however, that in his delusional state, Foster could have been a target herself.

"She definitely could have been a target, it’s just fate went the other way," Hinckley said. "But, yeah, she could have been a target. But as fate turned out, it was Reagan instead of her."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In a 2022 interview with CBS, Hinckley apologized for his actions.

Jodie Foster is seen on the set of "Taxi Driver" with Robert De Niro and director Martin Scorsese. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"I shot four people, and I’m sorry to the Reagan family, the Brady family, the other families of the victims," he said at the time. "I’m sorry to Jodie Foster for bringing her into this."

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Europe solar eclipse live: millions flock to viewing spots in Spain, UK and Iceland
excerpt:
Eclipse to be witnessed by tens of millions across western Europe as enthusiasts gather along path of totality

Do not fret if not. Not everyone is prepared like this guy.

Welcome to the live coverag...
body_text:
Eclipse to be witnessed by tens of millions across western Europe as enthusiasts gather along path of totality

Do not fret if not. Not everyone is prepared like this guy.

Welcome to the live coverage of today’s total eclipse, which will be seen in parts of Europe, including Iceland, the UK, and Spain.

Tips on how to view the phenomenon safely

First-hand reports from places where crowds are gathering

A quick look at the science behind the shadow

The best pictures and videos from key viewing spots

And yes, there will be a live stream, too.

It’s Wednesday, 12 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

For several days, Mount Etna, one of the world’s most active volcanoes, has been putting on a spectacular display, spewing incandescent magma, sending long streams of lava down its slopes and showering the surrounding area with ash.

Explosive activity has been recorded on Etna’s north-eastern flank, where new fractures have opened, while the Voragine crater has continued to produce towering plumes of ash reaching heights of about 4,500 metres.

The latest eruptive phase on Europe’s highest active volcano was continuing from vents at altitudes of 2,750 metres (9,022ft) and 2,360 metres, feeding several lava flows and creating extensive lava fields, according to Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology (INGV).

INGV’s Volcano Observatory Notice for Aviation (VONA) remained at red, its highest alert level, indicating an ongoing risk to aircraft from ash emissions.

The volcanic ash has caused widespread disruption at Catania airport, forcing the cancellation of numerous flights. On Tuesday, the ash cloud drifted as far as Malta, about 220km (140 miles) south of Etna, forcing airlines to cancel flights to the Mediterranean island at the height of the tourist season.

At the same time, the eruptions have drawn thousands of tourists to Etna, fascinated by the spectacle of fire and glowing lava illuminating the volcano after dark.

In recent years, experts have observed that Etna has been spewing so-called “primitive magma”, a term used to describe magma whose composition has changed relatively little from that of the Earth’s mantle where it formed. Rising from deeper within the volcano, this magma carries a greater concentration of gas and is therefore capable of producing the spectacularly high lava fountains that have become a feature of Etna’s recent eruptions.

While tonight’s eclipse will the “the greatest show off earth,” as the Guardian called it the last time it happened in 1999, it’s not the only show around.

You can check the expected eclipse timings at your location using special websites offered by various European metereological services, like this one.

In Iceland, the show will begin earlier than elsewhere: around 4.45pm local time (5.45pm UK time), and end just before 7pm (8pm).

At the Guardian HQ in London, the partial eclipse will begin at 6.17pm, reach its maximum stage at 7.13pm, and end at 8.06pm.

And Spain will be again a bit later than the UK.

The roads and car parks of west and north Cornwall are clogged as people gather to watch the solar eclipse.

Residents and holidaymakers are set to witness about 95% coverage – about 5% more than London according to the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.

And, yes, there is a shortage of eclipse glasses. There were notices on shops in Penzance saying they had none; in St Ives, dozens of people queued at a phone repair shop when it announced a new batch had arrived.

The eclipse comes with health warnings. The Falmouth coastguard has told people not to get too close to cliffs as the darkness gathers while the RNLI is advising those intending to watch from kayaks or surfboards or take an eclipse dip in the sea to remember that it is going to turn a little colder and, of course, visibility will be poorer.

There was a full eclipse in Cornwall in 1999 and civic leaders spent two years planning for it but poor weather meant there wasn’t the influx of visitors that had been expected.

Twenty seven years (and one day on), the vibe is a little more laid back but fine weather means the view of the eclipse should be excellent.

I can confirm that eclipse glasses are also in short supply here in Madrid.

Our local library had run out of the free glasses supplied by the city council two days ago, and an inquiry at a nearby optician was met with a rather curt “agotadas” (all gone) before we’d got to the end of the sentence.

Safety recalls have also been issued over six models of eclipse glasses that had been on sale here.

We’ve managed to buy some online and are getting ready for tonight in the mountains north of Madrid.

Younger members of the family are already impatient. It’s going to be a long, hot few hours…

The last significant partial eclipse was reported in the UK in 1999.

Here is how we covered it at the time at the Guardian:

“Britain was brought to a standstill for almost an hour yesterday as millions of people left their homes, offices and factories to watch the last eclipse of the millennium.

The rush to watch the skies in the West Country and across the country resulted in the biggest power surge ever recorded on the National Grid and is estimated to have cost the country £500m in lost business.

More than a million people gathered in Cornwall and Devon for the once-in-a-lifetime event, with a last minute dash to the West Country by an estimated 60,000, bringing the total number of visitors to Cornwall to 270,000, double the normal number for August.”

For many, though, it was down to the luck of the meteorological draw whether they actually succeeded in glimpsing the eclipse through the thick cloud covering the counties.

For many, umbrellas rather than solar eclipse viewers were needed when, an hour before the eclipse, a torrential rainstorm lashed west Cornwall and heavy cloud completely blocked the view.

While the Scillies enjoyed 106 seconds of totality under clear skies, the thousands gathered in Penzance, Marazion and Falmouth found cloud and rain blotted out their view.

Within an hour of the eclipse, more than 100 people called a helpline at Moorfields Eye Hospital in London, complaining of problems after watching the solar spectacular.

Many hospitals cancelled eye operations to make way for emergencies and will remain on 24-hour standby until the weekend for worried eclipse watchers who fear they have damaged their vision.”

It’s nice of Bónus bosses to offer their employees a chance to go out and experience the eclipse.

For all we know, there isn’t usually that much interest in supermarket shopping during the phenomenon – with Waitrose chief even complaining about it in 1999, the last time we had a solar eclipse in the UK…

In Iceland, people have flocked by air, land and sea to watch the total solar eclipse – the country’s first in 72 years.

But the forecast is not looking promising, with low clouds expected to cover much of the country.

The eclipse will start in Iceland at about 4.45pm local time (5.45pm UK) and end at about 6.50pm (7.50pm UK).

The total eclipse will only be visible in western Iceland, with the longest in Látrabjarg in the Westfjords where it will last for 2 minutes and 13 seconds. A road in the area was closed overnight due to heavy traffic and people were not permitted to stay at the site, which is part of a nature reserve, overnight.

Record numbers of cruise ships are headed to the water around Iceland in the hope of witnessing the eclipse.

The Icelandic artist Björk is hosting a one-day festival to coincide with the eclipse at Hafnarfjörður near Reykjavík. The eclipse is featured in the set list at 5.48pm between DJ sets by Arca and Björk.

The boss of supermarket Bónuss has told store managers they can close for 15 minutes to allow employees to see the eclipse.

A wide band of north and central Spain, plus a sliver of Portugal and parts of Greenland and Iceland will experience a rare total eclipse.

The light of the setting sun will be virtually blocked out across much of western Europe, including the UK, France, Belgium, Switzerland and northern Italy.

This total eclipse will be the first in mainland Europe in two decades.

The last event of this kind visible from the UK occurred in 1999, when parts of Devon and Cornwall were in the path of totality.

The next total solar eclipse visible in the UK is not due to occur until 2090.

The online forums are abuzz as people debate potential cloud cover and trade tips on the best viewing points. Hours before wide swathes of Spain were set to experience the country’s first total solar eclipse in more than a century, the excitement was palpable.

“It’s going to be spectacular,” said César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium. “A total solar eclipse is one of the best spectacles in nature.”

Officials have estimated that as many as 6 million people could flock to the eclipse path on Wednesday, which stretches about 200km from A Coruña in Spain’s northwest to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. A small strip of Portugal and parts of Greenland and Iceland will also experience the rare total eclipse.

Tens of millions more will be watching across western Europe, with the path of the eclipse virtually blocking out the sun in many countries including the UK, France, Belgium, Switzerland and northern Italy.

Do not fret if not. Not everyone is prepared like this guy.

Welcome to the live coverage of today’s total eclipse, which will be seen in parts of Europe, including Iceland, the UK, and Spain.

Tips on how to view the phenomenon safely

First-hand reports from places where crowds are gathering

A quick look at the science behind the shadow

The best pictures and videos from key viewing spots

And yes, there will be a live stream, too.

It’s Wednesday, 12 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: Mamdani's team said NYPD would accompany his wife on Middle East vacation — cops say that's not true
excerpt: Police security escorts are denied for the wife of NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani during her upcoming trip to Lebanon and Syria. Nate Foy breaks down the NYPD decision. Mamdani's office initially claimed se...
body_text:
Police security escorts are denied for the wife of NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani during her upcoming trip to Lebanon and Syria. Nate Foy breaks down the NYPD decision. Mamdani's office initially claimed security would join her, later blaming a miscommunication.

The New York Police Department (NYPD) will not provide a security detail to Mayor Zohran Mamdani's wife during her upcoming vacation to two terror hotspots in the Middle East, despite the mayor's office claiming otherwise.

"The NYPD does not send officers to countries with level 4 travel advisories for discretionary reasons such as personal travel," a spokesperson for the law enforcement agency told Fox News.

Mamdani's wife, Rama Duwaji, is planning to travel to Syria and Lebanon to visit family in September, according to the New York Post. Both of those countries are on the State Department's "Do Not Travel" list due to terrorism concerns.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his wife, Rama Duwaji, smile as confetti falls after his ceremonial inauguration as mayor at City Hall on Jan. 1, 2026, in New York. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)

MAMDANI'S WIFE CO-HOSTS LUXE MUSLIM RETREAT CASTING VIRGIN MARY AS ‘PALESTINIAN WOMAN’ UNDER OCCUPATION

The mayor's office had previously confirmed that Duwaji would have an NYPD security detail on the trip.

"Upon the strong recommendation of the NYPD, the first lady’s security detail will be joining her when she travels to visit family in Syria and Lebanon," Mamdani’s spokeswoman Dora Pekec reportedly said.

But later, as it became clear that the NYPD would not be making the overseas trek, the mayor chalked the confusion up to a staff "miscommunication" when asked about it by news outlet PIX11 on Tuesday.

NYPD Detectives’ Endowment Association (DEA) President Scott Munro furiously slammed the implication that NYPD detectives would accompany the city's First Lady to the Middle East.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch speak at a Sunday morning news conference after a spate of weekend shootings in Brooklyn. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu)

MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS

"Our detectives put themselves in harm’s way every day protecting New Yorkers," said Munro. "The DEA would never remain silent if our members were asked to travel to a dangerous, off-limits foreign country for anything other than a legitimate law-enforcement or intelligence operation."

"Our detectives are needed here in New York City protecting residents and fighting crime," he added.

Mamdani has a long history of trashing the very police department he thought would accompany and provide security for his wife to the dangerous Middle Eastern countries on New York City taxpayer's dime.

"There is no negotiating with an institution this wicked & corrupt. Defund it. Dismantle it. End the cycle of violence," Mamdani said in reference to the NYPD in a viral 2020 post on X.

Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, holds up bananas labeled with a 30% off sticker during an announcement on municipal grocery stores at a Campaign for Hunger community food distribution center in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Monday, July 27, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"We don't need an investigation to know that the NYPD is racist, anti-queer & a major threat to public safety," he said in another 2020 post, adding in a follow-up: "What we need is to #DefundTheNYPD."

JON STEWART PRESSES MAMDANI ON WHERE HE BREAKS WITH FELLOW DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ON PRISONS AND BORDERS

"Queer liberation means defund the police," he said in yet another post.

The mayor, who has also faced scrutiny for his anti-Israel views and recently called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" while calling for his arrest, derogatorily linked the NYPD to the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF).

"We have to make clear that when the boot of the NYPD is on your neck, it’s been laced by the IDF," Mamdani, who was a keynote speaker, said during a panel discussion at the Democratic Socialists of America's 2023 national convention.

Jessica Tisch speaks after being sworn in as the next Commissioner of the New York Police Department (NYPD) during a ceremony at One Police Plaza on November 25, 2024, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

During his campaign for mayor of the most populated U.S. city, Mamdani said the exact opposite, explicitly stating that he did not want to defund the police.

SEE IT: MAMDANI BOOED OFF STAGE AT NEW YORK CITY PRO-POLICE CELEBRATION: ‘WALKED OFF IN SHAME’

Still, it appears there is no love lost between Mamdani and the NYPD.

Just last week, he was booed offstage when he tried to speak at a pro-police event in Staten Island.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Alex Rodriguez defends Dodgers' spending spree as likely lockout gets closer: 'I think it's great'
excerpt:
After MLB owners offered a salary cap for the first time since 1994, NFL star Saquon Barkley recently spoke to Fox News Digital and shared his full support for the players.

With a lockout more likely...
body_text:
After MLB owners offered a salary cap for the first time since 1994, NFL star Saquon Barkley recently spoke to Fox News Digital and shared his full support for the players.

With a lockout more likely than not at this point in Major League Baseball, the ongoing debate continues over whether the Los Angeles Dodgers are actually ruining the sport.

Many believe the Dodgers have simply broken baseball, particularly with Shohei Ohtani's $700 million contract, 97% of which is deferred. They have won back-to-back World Series titles and are the favorite for a third consecutive title.

Not only did Los Angeles follow up its titles by signing the most touted reliever on the market in Edwin Diaz, but it also gave Kyle Tucker a deal that gave him the highest annual average value of $60 million, the most for any position player ever.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Alex Rodriguez reacts during the Seattle Mariners 50th Season Celebration at T-Mobile Park on Aug. 8, 2026, in Seattle, Washington. (Jack Compton/Getty Images)

However, former slugger Alex Rodriguez isn't buying the negativity surrounding the organization.

"I think it’s great. You and I both would be hypocrites if we said it’s not good when we saw what happened in the ‘90s here in New York, what happened in ‘09 when Hal Steinbrenner flexed his financial resources to go out and get [CC] Sabathia, [Mark] Teixeira and A.J. Burnett, and the year before we had Johnny Damon," A-Rod told New York Yankees broadcaster Michael Kay on the latter's radio show.

Rodriguez does make an interesting point — in 2005, the Yankees' payroll ($208.3 million, per Baseball Reference) was almost double the second-highest payroll (the Boston Red Sox's $123.5 million). The New York Mets ($101.3 million) were the only other team to have a nine-digit payroll.

While the Dodgers have finessed their contracts through deferrals and bonuses to make their actual payroll less than the actual value of the contracts, numerous other teams are actually still in the comparative ballpark. The Mets, Philadelphia Phillies and Toronto Blue Jays each have a tax payroll of at least $300 million.

Rodriguez noted that it's not necessarily the amount of money but how it's spent.

Former New York Yankee Alex Rodriguez attends the team's Old Timer's Day prior to a game against the Colorado Rockies at Yankee Stadium on Aug. 24, 2024, in New York City. (Jim McIsaac/Getty Images)

FORMER MLB STAR CALLS FOR SALARY FIX AS OWNERS, PLAYERS ASSOCIATION TALK 'TWO DIFFERENT LANGUAGES'

"The key is not making the mistakes..." Rodriguez said, name-dropping Trent Grisham and Ryan McMahon, who are combining to make $38 million this season while hitting a combined .215 with an OPS below .700.

"You have to be able to determine what is your inventory and what is it worth. Gene Michael used to be able to hold on to Bernie [Williams], [Derek] Jeter, [Jorge] Posada. That's the key - you got to hold on to your early guys, and then move on for the others, use them as assets to complement your current roster."

Again to Rodriguez's point, the Milwaukee Brewers, whose $153 million tax payroll is 19th in the league, own the best record in Major League Baseball. The Tampa Bay Rays rank 27th in tax payroll yet have the league's second-best record, while the AL Central-leading Chicago White Sox rank 26th.

Furthermore, three of the top five payrolls in the sport — the Mets, Phillies and Blue Jays — are currently out of the postseason.

Alex Rodriguez #13 of the New York Yankees celebrates after the Yankees' 7-3 win against the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 6 of the 2009 MLB World Series at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx, New York City, on Nov. 4, 2009. (Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images)

The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, and players have insisted they would not play under a salary cap, which has been formally offered for the first time since 1994.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X, and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

title: Burnham to consider ban on disposable barbecues as wildfires rage in UK
excerpt:
PM to look at imposing restriction on devices in public spaces, though campaigners fear it does not go far enough

The government will look at banning disposable barbecues as wildfires continue to rag...
body_text:
PM to look at imposing restriction on devices in public spaces, though campaigners fear it does not go far enough

The government will look at banning disposable barbecues as wildfires continue to rage across the UK, Andy Burnham has said.

Disposable barbecues have been the cause of a number of serious fires over the last few years, but campaigners were critical of the prime minister’s failure to link those fires more broadly to the climate crisis.

In July this year, firefighters called to Cannock Chase found an area the size of a football field blazing in the summer heat. The heathland in Sherbrook Valley, part of a special area of conservation, was home to adders, toads and other wildlife, which were thought to have suffered severe damage, though no people were harmed. The cause of the fire was identified as a disposable barbecue.

This was one of two fires in the area that were particularly concerning, Staffordshire council officials said, because Cannock Chase is home to protected wildlife, including ground-nesting nightjars. Fires can destroy nests, chicks and vital heathland habitat, causing damage that can take many years to recover from.

Disposable barbecues, which can be carried into public areas, present a number of problems: they remain hot, sometimes for hours, after they are used, making them extremely difficult to dispose of safely, and when they cannot be carried away, people are forced to leave them or place them into bins where they carry on smouldering.

Burying the barbecues, as some try to do, will not stop the danger as these trays of charcoal can reach 450C and will carry on burning underground, where they can still ignite fires long after use. On beaches, the buried coals and metal grills are also a hazard for walkers, and in fields for farm animals.

Over the last few years they have been identified as the cause of a number of serious fires including:

Macclesfield, Cheshire, July 2026: a large woodland fire that was tackled by dozens of firefighters. Cheshire fire and rescue service said a discarded barbecue was the probable cause

Three separate fires in one day around London, July 2026: in Feltham, 6 hectares of heathland close to houses were damaged. The London fire brigade urged people not to use disposable barbecues and to properly extinguish cigarettes after crews tackled three grass fires.

The Trossachs, Scotland, May 2025: covered 2 hectares in the Glen Finglas region of the national park. Glen Finglas is the biggest Woodland Trust site in the UK. The barbecue understood to have sparked that fire was found with a burger still on the grill.

The National Farmers’ Union is now calling for a ban. Although Burnham has said he may consider a ban, government ministers have been set against such measures.

A spokesperson for the government said: “There are no plans to introduce a blanket ban on disposable barbecues. We take the risk of fires very seriously, which is why we’ve taken action to make disposable barbecues safer to use, including making sure they follow strict product safety rules and giving councils the power to ban them in high-risk areas.”

Jon Pearce, the Labour MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, 50 miles from Cannock Chase, has been working on ways to bring forward a partial restriction on the devices in legislation, which would avoid some of the problems of a blanket ban.

He said: “It is hugely welcome that the prime minister has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues. He is right that the message needs to go out loud and clear that people should not be using disposable barbecues in public places at this time.

“But we need to be in a better place next summer. Last year was the worst on record for wildfires. This year will surpass it. We need to accept our climate has changed and put in place measures to adapt, and one of those is banning the use of disposable barbecues in public places.”

Portable barbecues could be exempt, he said, as they were taken away after use. “The irony of ‘disposable barbecues’ is that they are actually very difficult to dispose of. They can cause bin fires, and unless you stay around for a long time until it has totally cooled down, there is still a fire risk.”

Other igniters for fire include lightning strikes, carelessly tossed cigarettes, campfires, rubbish and bottles. But it is clear that disposable barbecues pose particular problems. Research for the government published last year found more than 1,600 fires were caused by barbecues in England from 2020 to 2024, though it did not specify whether those barbecues were disposable, and the cause of a majority of the nearly 4,500 fires listed was put down as unknown.

The Greenpeace political campaigner Angharad Hopkinson said: “To truly protect the public, the government must also address the fossil-fuelled elephant in the room that is driving extreme temperatures. The climate crisis is staring us in the face, threatening our national security and straining our resilience to breaking point.

“Burnham has acknowledged the dangers of these conditions by convening Cobra; now he must match that urgency with a real long-term plan to end our reliance on fossil fuels – the ultimate driver of climate change – once and for all.”

title: David Crowley vows to earn support from progressives after winning messy Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor – live
excerpt:
David Crowley speaks after accepting Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor; progressive Francesca Hong had led polls by a large margin in election lead-up

David Crowley wins Wisconsin Democrat...
body_text:
David Crowley speaks after accepting Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor; progressive Francesca Hong had led polls by a large margin in election lead-up

David Crowley wins Wisconsin Democratic primary for governor

At a press conference on Wednesday, David Crowley accepted the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor, and vowed to unite a fractured coalition heading into November’s general election.

He thanked Francesca Hong, his progressive challenger, noting that her campaign “reminded people across Wisconsin that there are no long shots in believing in a better future and fighting to expand opportunities to every family.”

He welcomed those who voted for her in Tuesday’s primary to join him in the lead up to November.

“I look forward to earning their support,” Crowley told reporters.

The newly minted nominee said that while the messy Democratic primary has been branded as a “battle between the left and the center”, it’s ultimately an inaccurate characterization.

“We may not agree on every policy. We may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable health care, good-paying jobs, and a brighter future for all of our children,” he said.

He added: “Every one of us has something much bigger to unite around, and that is keeping Maga extremism from bringing the chaos we see in Washington into our neighborhoods right here in the state of Wisconsin.”

Donald Trump continued to insist that the US has “total control” of the strait of Hormuz, despite cargo traffic through the vital waterway only a fraction of what it was before the war began in February.

Trump said that he thinks the US will “KEEP” control of the chokepoint. “Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, ‘A WALL OF STEEL,’ and there is nothing Iran can do about it,” the president added. “They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, their remaining soldiers are unpaid … Iran is all talk and no action, the Bully of the Middle East No Longer. Praise be to Allah!”

The Trump administration has finalized a rule ending federal Medicaid funding for gender‑affirming care for transgender minors.

Under the policy, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services will bar states from seeking federal reimbursement for what the administration calls “sex‑rejecting procedures”. In practice, that includes puberty blockers – which are reversible – hormone therapy, and, in rare cases, surgeries for trans youth.

The rule takes effect 13 October. Beneficiaries will have up to six months to claim coverage for hormone therapy medications after that date. Federal funding for talk therapy related to gender dysphoria will continue.

“We are not going to pay for our innocent children to undergo these barbaric surgeries and practices, which result in unthinkable and irreversible harm to their young bodies,” Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The move marks the latest step in the White House’s broader effort to strip federal support from providers treating trans youth, despite gender‑affirming care being endorsed by major US and international medical associations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics. Providers stress that treatment plans follow extensive evaluations and involve families throughout.

Trump claimed that “dozens of U.S. hospitals have already ended this so‑called ‘gender‑affirming care,’” citing pressure from his administration. Earlier this year, STAT news reported that more than 40 hospitals have paused or stopped some services for trans youth since Trump returned to office. In February, the Guardian reported that NYU Langone Health, one of New York City’s major hospital networks, would shut down its gender‑affirming care program for minors.

The new rule leans on a Department of Health and Human Services report that questions the medical consensus that gender‑affirming care can be life‑saving for transgender youth.

When Crowley was asked how he plans to get progressives on board, he said that that he wants to engage with voters “no matter where you fall on the political spectrum”.

“So many people have felt like they’ve been on the menu because nobody has asked them to lend their voices to the solutions,” Crowley added, while noting his ultimate goal is to beat his Republican challenger, congressman Tom Tiffany, in November.

At a press conference on Wednesday, David Crowley accepted the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor, and vowed to unite a fractured coalition heading into November’s general election.

He thanked Francesca Hong, his progressive challenger, noting that her campaign “reminded people across Wisconsin that there are no long shots in believing in a better future and fighting to expand opportunities to every family.”

He welcomed those who voted for her in Tuesday’s primary to join him in the lead up to November.

“I look forward to earning their support,” Crowley told reporters.

The newly minted nominee said that while the messy Democratic primary has been branded as a “battle between the left and the center”, it’s ultimately an inaccurate characterization.

“We may not agree on every policy. We may not use the same labels, but we all want safe communities, strong schools, affordable health care, good-paying jobs, and a brighter future for all of our children,” he said.

He added: “Every one of us has something much bigger to unite around, and that is keeping Maga extremism from bringing the chaos we see in Washington into our neighborhoods right here in the state of Wisconsin.”

Some Alabama voters took to the polls for the second time this primary season after the state’s Republican-controlled legislature reconfigured four of the seven districts.

The redrawn district map came after the US supreme court dismantled a key section of the 1965 Voting Rights Act and several southern states moved to redistrict and consolidate Republican power. In June, the supreme court ruled that Alabama could use a redrawn congressional map that eliminates one of the state’s two majority-Black districts in this year’s midterm elections.

The new map poses steep challenges for Shomari Figures, the Democratic representative who was first elected in 2024 after the creation of a new district that included the mostly Black cities of Mobile and Montgomery. But the district no longer includes Mobile, Figures’s home town. Rhett Marques, a Republican state representative and small-business owner who became part of the new district, won the primary to challenge Figures in November.

Here’s a round-up of some of the key takeaways from Tuesday’s primaries:

Michael Alfonso, the son-in-law of transportation secretary Sean Duffy, won the Republican nomination for Wisconsin’s seventh congressional district.

The seat is currently held by Tom Tiffany, who as we noted earlier, ran unopposed for the GOP nomination for governor.

Alfonso, 26, received Donald Trump’s support for the primary and won in a landslide – beating four other Republican candidates in a red district that was represented by Duffy from 2011-2020, when he left Congress

Tony Evers, the outgoing Wisconsin governor, praised David Crowley on his victory in Tuesday’s Democratic primary for the governor’s race.

“He’s the future of our party,” Evers said. “I can’t wait for him to be our next governor.”

Evers’ endorsement spurred Crowley to re-enter the race in July, after the Milwaukee county executive initially suspended his bid.

Crowley will now face Tom Tiffany, a Trump-endorsed Republican congressman who ran unopposed in the Republican primary.

Core inflation, which measures prices without volatile goods like food and gas, rose by 0.2% in July, after not really changing in June compared to the month prior.

While the latest data shows there has been a 2.9% drop in gas prices from June to July, there has been a 25% hike compared to this time last year.

Prices in the US rose by 0.1% in July, with overall inflation up 3.4% compared to a year ago, according to the latest consumer price index report released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Donald Trump is in Washington today. He’ll spend the day in private meetings. At 10.30am ET he’ll meet with military service members and law enforcement. That’s currently closed to the press but we’ll let you know if that changes.

We’ll also be keeping an eye out on his reaction to Tuesday’s key primary results.

The World Health Organization has warned that Donald Trump’s bid to overhaul child vaccination in the United States went against “decades of evidence”.

President Trump signed an order Monday pushing for a rethink of school vaccine mandates and repeating calls for the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to be separated into three separate shots.

His health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr founded an anti-vaccine group and has long promoted a disproven link between the MMR shot and autism, AFP reported.

But WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the science is “unequivocal: vaccines – including the MMR vaccine – are safe and do not cause autism.”

“Vaccination policy should be guided by rigorous, independent and transparent review of the best available science, not by political influence,” he warned in a post on X.

He said that the WHO is “concerned that recent changes to US immunisation policy are not aligned with decades of evidence that show when children are most vulnerable to disease.”

Senator Darline Graham, appointed to complete the Senate term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham of South Carolina will face congressman Ralph Norman in a runoff election for the Republican nomination.

Graham held a narrow lead in the polls going into the abbreviated special primary on Tuesday, which predicted a close contest for second place. Norman, Russell Fry, a congressman, and Mark Sanford, a former governor, had polled within a point of each other in the most recent survey from the Trafalgar Group.

The winner of the runoff on 25 August will face Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, in November.

Graham has loudly trumpeted her endorsement from Donald Trump, but also enjoys the support of South Carolina’s governor, Henry McMaster, and John Thune, the Senate majority leader. In recent interviews the political outsider sought to convince people that her experience, and focus on affordability, made her the right candidate.

“I ran a state agency. I turned it from a struggling agency into a national model. I think that’s great experience to bring to the table,” Graham said, addressing reporters after casting her ballot on Tuesday. She highlighted the passage of a sanctions bill targeting Russia during her short tenure in Washington. “I was the deciding vote on Todd Blanche as attorney general. So I think I’ve accomplished a whole lot in three weeks.”

President Donald Trump’s administration is to spend ⁠at least $900m ​for construction projects on the White House grounds, ⁠the Washington Post reported on Wednesday, citing records.

Instead of ⁠securing money directly from ​Congress, the administration ‌has gathered ‌funding from other agencies and private ‌donors and directed it to an account that holds a few million dollars for routine maintenance of the ‌White House, the report said.

Confidential contracts and related ​planning documents indicate that the administration plans to use money in that account for White ⁠House “modernization projects,” the report added.

In July, Donald Trump hid in a catering truck and reportedly secretly switched planes in a security ruse prompted by a credible Iranian assassination threat.

In this video, the Guardian breaks down the footage from that day, showing how the president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras and then was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight.

Trump’s actual location was concealed from journalists and some White House staff, who thought they were traveling with Trump on the older plane.

Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in a race centered on immigration enforcement after the Trump administration crackdown turned deadly and destructive earlier this year.

Flanagan ousted congresswoman Angie Craig in yet another example of progressive campaigns toppling moderates amid an anti-establishment wave among Democrats.

“It’s time to fight for what people actually need,” Flanagan recently told the Guardian. “And so often I think Democrats are like: ‘What do we think we can win?’ Instead of: ‘What are the fights that we should be picking?’”

Flanagan will now face Michele Tafoya, a Republican former National Football League sideline reporter, in November. If she wins, Flanagan will become the first Native American woman in the Senate.

Meanwhile, the state’s gubernatorial race proved a rebuke of Donald Trump’s endorsement power as Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, lost to Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota house speaker. Demuth will face Amy Klobuchar, a Democratic US senator, in November, where Klobuchar is favored to win.

Lindell’s significant campaign liabilities had led his own party to speak out against his campaign. He is contending with ongoing defamation cases because of his election denialism, as well as a potential campaign finance violation for handing out free pillows at a parade. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, which faces legal claims for unpaid bills.

Minnesota leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor and a Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972.

David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, won the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor after beating the Democratic socialist Francesca Hong.

Crowley pulled off a last-minute victory after re-entering the campaign and snagging an endorsement from Tony Evers, the outgoing governor.

With most votes counted, Crowley had 39.8% of the vote, ahead of Hong’s 39.4%, according to the Associated Press: a lead of just more than 3,000 votes. The race came down to the wire, with Hong and Crowley running close to each other as each batch of results came in.

Polls had shown Hong as a clear frontrunner during the campaign, but with large chunks of voters still undecided and an ever-changing field of candidates, polling was difficult. Polls in Michigan had similarly shown the progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed with a more sizeable lead than he ended up with in his victory in the Democratic primary for US Senate.

Crowley’s pitch to voters in the waning weeks of the campaign was electability: he felt he was more poised to win against Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Tiffany voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost.

double quotation markWe knew that the stakes were too high for me to sit on the sideline, and that we need the best candidate, not just with executive leadership, but somebody who has a proven track record of getting things done. And that’s what voters want. They want someone they can trust. And that’s why we got back into this race.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump said he slipped away from Air Force One after a trip last month in Turkey because the Secret Service and military wanted him on a “different plane” due to a threat that he insisted didn’t scare him.

When US intelligence allegedly found a credible threat that Iran plotted to kill him last month, Trump left Air Force One in a catering truck, an episode first reported by the Washington Post and also by the New York Times.

Trump downplayed the extraordinary nature of the subterfuge, as well as the risk to the people – White House officials, security and support staff, and reporters – he left on the plane.

“They wanted me to go on a different flight, different plane,” Trump told reporters after returning from an event in Ohio, saying he had little choice in the matter.

“I guess there was a threat out there. I didn’t really ask too much about it,” he said. “I get a lot of threats.”

While the president was reportedly snuck out the side door of the plane, more than a hundred aides, officials and reporters were kept onboard to fly towards Britain, without being told there was a threat to their lives.

It comes as Democrats called for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade. Critics now question why reporters and the public had been deliberately misled.

“It appears that the idea was we can reduce the danger to president Trump by offering up 100 or so people to be killed by the Iranians in his place,” said Steven Cash, executive director of the Steady State and a former CIA intelligence officer and senior adviser to the Department of Homeland Security’s intelligence branch.

Richard Blumenthal, a Democratic senator for Connecticut, called the operation “unprecedented and surreal” and “downright scary” on CNN. “There has to be a congressional briefing because it involves not just the safety of the president.

“I want to know what precautions were taken to make sure that all of the passengers on that Air Force One, which was judged too dangerous for the president to fly on, what precautions were taken to keep the staff and reporters on that plane safe?”

David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, pulled off a last-minute victory after re-entering the Wisconsin governor’s race and snagging an endorsement from Tony Evers, the outgoing governor. The race came down to the wire, with Francesca Hong and Crowley running close to each other as each batch of results came in. Republican Tom Tiffany easily secured his party’s nomination.

In Minnesota, lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan handily won the Democratic primary for US Senate, beating moderate US representative Angie Craig in a race animated by anti-ICE sentiment. She will face Michele Tafoya in the general.

In the Republican bid for Minnesota governor, House speaker Lisa Demuth scored an upset, beating pillow salesman Mike Lindell, who had gotten Trump’s endorsement. She will face Amy Klobuchar in the general.

And in hotly contested congressional races:

Luke Bronin beat incumbent John Larson in Connecticut’s first congressional district.

Matt Little won a three-way race in Craig’s district, Minnesota’s third congressional district.

Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic primary in her third try to unseat Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s toss-up third congressional district.

title: Dem in key swing race missed nearly half her state House votes while taking taxpayer salary: 'No show'
excerpt: Christina Bohannan warned in 2021 that Iowa would become a "backwater" if lawmakers barred transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. Iowa enacted the ban in 2022. (Credit: YouTube/City of I...
body_text:
Christina Bohannan warned in 2021 that Iowa would become a "backwater" if lawmakers barred transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. Iowa enacted the ban in 2022. (Credit: YouTube/City of Iowa City - April 2, 2021)

FIRST ON FOX: Former Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan missed nearly half of her votes in Iowa's House of Representatives during her final year in office as she campaigned for a congressional seat in the battleground district, records show.

In 2022, Bohannan missed 348 of 773 floor votes, or about 45% of all votes, according to the legislature’s records, despite stressing the importance "for leaders to show up" three years later.

Bohannan is currently running for Congress in Iowa's 1st Congressional District, a race that Cook Political Report ranks as a "toss up" in November as Republicans attempt to preserve their razor-thin majority in the House of Representatives.

Some of the skipped votes involved bills addressing protections for sexual abuse victims, volunteer firefighters and first responders, Iowa’s dairy industry, agricultural programs, emergency 911 services, and juvenile justice reform.

IOWA DEM WHO TOUTED 'STRONG WORK ETHIC' MISSES MORE THAN HALF OF HER HOUSE VOTES

Former Iowa Democratic state Rep. Christina Bohannan missed nearly half of her state House votes while campaigning for Congress, records show. (Iowa Legislature ; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Liberal Christina Bohannan says leaders should ‘show up’ and then is a no-show herself," Emily Tuttle, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Missing half your job while collecting your taxpayer-funded paycheck isn’t leadership worthy of a promotion — it’s the kind of performance that would get you fired anywhere else."

The absences stand in contrast with Bohannan’s past comments. In an Oct. 6, 2025, post on X, she wrote that she had the "honor of speaking" with more than 100 voters at a candidate forum representing five Iowa counties, adding, "At a time when so much is uncertain, it’s more important than ever for leaders to show up and talk directly with Iowans."

Similarly, in a 2021 interview with Bleeding Heartland, an Iowa politics blog, Bohannan was described as planning to spend "a lot of time on legislative work during the 2022 session," with the rest of her efforts focused on her congressional campaign.

Bohannan served one term in the Iowa House from 2021 to 2023 before launching her first campaign for Congress.

BATTLEGROUND DEM CALLED PATRIOTISM 'SENSITIVE AND CONTROVERSIAL' DURING DEBATE OVER THE PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE

Christina Bohannan, candidate for Iowa’s first congressional district, listens during a roundtable on affordable housing Wednesday, Oct. 23, 2024 in Iowa City, Iowa. (Iowa City Press-Citizen)

She is now challenging incumbent Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, for a third time in the 1st Congressional District, which includes Davenport and Iowa City, after losing by about seven points in 2022 and roughly 800 votes following a recount in 2024.

But Bohannan remained on the state’s legislative payroll during that period. According to state legislative records, Iowa lawmakers earned a $25,000 annual salary in 2022, plus $175 per day in per diem for up to 100 days, or $17,500.

The Democratic lawmaker has also faced mounting criticism for her past comments and middle-class messaging on the campaign trail.

'QUEEN OF DEI' RUNNING FOR CONGRESS RIPPED HER RURAL STATE AS 'BACKWARDS' ON PODCAST

Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, attends a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital previously reported that Bohannan warned Iowa could be seen as "backwards" over limits on diversity training at public schools and universities and "look like a backwater" over restrictions on transgender athletes. Other reports revealed that Bohannan and her husband owned a waterfront Sarasota, Florida, condo valued between $500,001 and $1 million, in addition to a $1.55 million Iowa City home while campaigning as a hard-working, middle-class advocate who understands what it's like "to still struggle to put food on the table."

Fox News Digital reached out to Bohannan’s campaign for comment.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

title: Cambridge agrees to hold independent inquiry into Jason Arday appointment
excerpt:
Vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice says she recognises the ‘difficult case’ has damaged the university

Cambridge University’s leadership has bowed to internal pressure for an independent investigation ...
body_text:
Vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice says she recognises the ‘difficult case’ has damaged the university

Cambridge University’s leadership has bowed to internal pressure for an independent investigation into its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor, with its vice-chancellor admitting the affair has damaged the institution.

Prof Deborah Prentice said she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case” but described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.

Senior Cambridge academics had called for the university to hold a fully independent inquiry into the circumstances around Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology of education, after the details of his career and life story were exposed to intense scrutiny.

The university initially defended him as the “victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility” but he resigned last week after a series of his claims were called into doubt.

In a letter to staff, Prentice said: “I know there is anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case … We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

“That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge.”

The university did not supply any details of the investigation’s membership or its terms of reference.

Prentice said the investigation’s findings would be used to review Cambridge’s appointment process for senior roles, and that its education faculty bore some responsibility for Arday’s selection. She also highlighted that Arday had held positions at Durham and Glasgow universities before applying to Cambridge for a professorial chair.

“As you are fully aware, appointments to senior academic roles, as in the case of the faculty of education and Jason Arday, are currently led at department level,” she said. “I note that Durham and Glasgow universities have announced that they are also investigating the circumstances surrounding the appointment of Jason Arday to academic posts there.”

However, academics at Cambridge said Prentice’s description of the appointment process was “nonsense”, with Arday’s appointment made by a board of electors that included a representative of the university’s leadership.

While Glasgow has publicly announced its own investigation into Arday’s selection, Durham University declined to endorse Prentice’s comments.

A spokesperson for Durham said: “Since the recent emergence of questions relating to the circumstances surrounding Jason Arday’s appointment to a chair at Cambridge University, we have looked into his appointment to a junior academic role at Durham in 2019. He was appointed following a standard, competitive recruitment process in which he met published criteria for the role.

“He left Durham over four years ago and no longer has any formal association with us. Allegations about plagiarism in his PhD did not surface until after he had left Durham.”

Prentice also recognised the effect of the controversy on other black and minority ethnic academics at Cambridge, after some had described the atmosphere as toxic.

“In light of the focus on this troubling case and the widespread commentary around it, I want to be very clear that we do not need the outcomes of an investigation to clearly and loudly affirm that our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community,” she said.

“This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge.

“The desire for quick answers and rapid responses is understandable, but we need to allow these reviews to complete their work effectively so we can learn from any mistakes and, where needed, improve our processes.”

Prentice joined Cambridge from Princeton University in 2023, several months after Arday’s appointment.

title: US consumer inflation slows in July as energy prices briefly retreat
excerpt:
United States consumer inflation has slowed in July amid a short retreat in energy prices and hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen.

Shipping continues to be severely disrupted since Iran esta...
body_text:
United States consumer inflation has slowed in July amid a short retreat in energy prices and hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen.

Shipping continues to be severely disrupted since Iran established a maritime “toll booth” in the strait shortly after the US and Israel launched a war against the country in late February.

Consumer inflation rose by 0.1 percent compared with this time last month but was 3.4 percent higher than this time a year ago, according to data released by the Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.

Inflation has been largely driven by fuel prices, which, despite a temporary reprieve, are rising. While energy prices declined 1.5 percent from this time last month, they are up 14.7 percent for the year.

“Energy prices have gone down in July because people thought perhaps the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz would end, but it didn’t.  If you look at the past 12 months, energy prices are now much higher than they were a year ago,” Michael Klein, professor of international economic affairs at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, told Al Jazeera.

Brent crude fell 7 percent last week but has jumped this week as hopes that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen faded. Brent crude oil futures rose 0.3 percent to $89.19 per barrel on Wednesday.

Petrol prices dropped 2.9 percent from last month but surged 39.1 percent from a year ago.

At the petrol pump, prices are rising after tumbling 9 cents last week.

The average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of petrol is $4.03, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. By comparison, it was $4.00 on Monday, $4.08 this time last week, $3.87 a month ago, and $2.98 per gallon on February 28 , when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

Food prices rose marginally in July by 0.1 percent for the month but were 3 percent higher than this time last year.

The inflation comes amid a lacklustre jobs report last week, where the US economy lost 23,000 jobs, with most losses in retail trade, local government (particularly in education), and hospitality, while healthcare made gains, according to the BLS.

Days earlier, the Jobs and Labor Turnover Report (JOLTS), also from the BLS, showed little change in the number of people leaving their jobs for new ones, continuing a so-called low-fire, low-hire environment.

These combined factors have put pressure on the Federal Reserve as it gauges the path forward to reach its goal of 2 percent inflation. In July, the central bank kept interest rates at 3.50–3.75 percent.

Economists are divided on whether rates will rise or remain unchanged during the next policy meeting slated for September 16, which would be the third under the new chairman, Kevin Warsh, who took over from Jerome Powell in May.

CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts a 61.6 percent chance of maintaining rates, while 38.4 percent believe that rates will increase to 3.75–4.00 percent.

US markets are responding. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 rose by 0.3 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average is 0.05 percent higher since the market opened.

Gold prices, which are generally considered a safe investment during times of economic uncertainty, are up by 1.4 percent to $4,428 an ounce.

The inflationary pressures are overshadowed by the upcoming midterm elections. There are only two more inflation reports before the election.

Meanwhile, Americans are divided on which party is better suited to handle the economy. Slightly more Americans, or 37 percent, believe that Democrats are better at handling the economy, as opposed to 36 percent who believe that Republicans are, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week.

title: As Strait of Hormuz transit drops, Trump again says US has ‘control’
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has doubled down on claims the United States maintains “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz, even as transit through the arterial waterway fell to a one-week ...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has doubled down on claims the United States maintains “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz, even as transit through the arterial waterway fell to a one-week low amid the US-Israel war with Iran.

Trump made the statement in a Truth Social post on Wednesday, reiterating a similar claim he made to reporters the day before as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict and fully re-open the strait have continued to stall.

“The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!” Trump said.

He went on to claim the ongoing US blockade of Iranian ports “is being called, by everyone, “A WALL OF STEEL,” and there is nothing Iran can do about it”.

“Iran is all talk and no action, the Bully of the Middle East No Longer,” Trump said, ending his message with, “Praise be to Allah!”

Despite the statement, Iran has continued to assert its influence over the strait as it has pursued talks with Oman on future management. Wider peace talks with the US have been largely paused amid the Iran-Oman talks, which do not include Washington.

Iran has said it will not allow full traffic in the strait until the US naval blockade is lifted, sanctions are lifted, and its assets are unfrozen.

While ships can still transit through the strait, they face several obstacles and heightened threats. That has caused the volume of traffic to drop dramatically.

Reuters news agency reported that just eight ships transited through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, far below the 130 to 140 ships pre-war rate. That was down from the previous ten-day average of about 12 ships, according to trade analytics platform Kpler data.

The US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28. The US and Iran signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at ending the conflict in June, but the agreement dissolved in mid July with both sides renewing attacks.

Fighting between the US and Israel has been mostly in recent days, with sporadic incidents. That included a US Navy military helicopter striking a Panama-flagged cargo vessel on Tuesday.

The Yemen-based Houthis have also opened a new front in the war, with attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Six people were killed in a Houthi attack on an Egyptian-owned ship on Tuesday, in the first deaths from such an attack.

title: Cooper warns NHS must prepare for regular heatwaves as Burnham holds emergency Cobra meeting – UK politics live
excerpt:
Health secretary says service must plan ahead in the same way as it does for winter crises as UK faces its fifth heatwave of the summer

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said that she has told...
body_text:
Health secretary says service must plan ahead in the same way as it does for winter crises as UK faces its fifth heatwave of the summer

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said that she has told NHS England to start planning ahead for summer heatwaves, just as it prepares every year for a crisis in the winter.

In an article published in the Mirror, Cooper says global heating means Britain will face heatwaves like the one we are going through now “with increasing frequency and increasing intensity”. And this puts extra pressure on the NHS, she says, referencing a report that said there were almost 3,000 excess deaths because of the heat in May and June.

Cooper, who is attending the meeting of the Cobra emergency committee this afternoon to discuss the extreme heat, says:

double quotation markDuring the heatwaves in May and June, we saw more than 2,800 lives lost because of the extreme heat, and this year is on track to see the highest ever number of heat-related deaths. My thoughts go out to every family who has lost loved ones …

Our NHS is used to gearing up for these kinds of pressures in winter. But we are going to need the same level of preparation in future summers. I have told the NHS to start drawing up summer plans now in the way they have traditionally done for winter.

Especially as all the same people who are most at risk when it is very cold are at risk in the extreme heat: older people, the youngest children, and people with existing conditions …

We know Britain will face heatwaves like this with increasing frequency and increasing intensity. So we have to take the health consequences much more seriously, so that everyone is ready when they come.

Cooper also says in her article that some of the £6.75bn being spent on improving NHS buildings will fund air conditioning.

Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, has defended his decision to sign an open letter in support of the now-discredited Cambridge professor Jason Arday.

In an interview with Radio 4’s PM programme, Polanski said that he defended Arday “up until the point he resigned” and that at the time he signed the open letter “it looked like Cambridge University had run an investigation into Jason Arday and that he’d been cleared”.

Asked if it was a mistake for him to back Arday before he knew the full facts, Polanski replied:

double quotation markTwo things can be true at once. The first thing is that it looked like Cambridge University had done an investigation and cleared him, so I think under those circumstances it was perfectly OK to say, if someone has been cleared, I’m going to stand with them.

Secondly, to recognise that there is a problem with racism in academia and there’s a lack of people of colour who are academic professors.

And it’s also, thirdly, true that it doesn’t help if we just push people to the front without the right credentials because they’re really keen to make sure that they’re filling some sort of quota.

I think we need to make sure that the right people are in the right jobs, and we also need to tackle racism in society. All of those things can be true at once.

In an interview with LBC yesterday, Andy Burnham declared that he was “a fan” of Greggs. This came as a conversation about government plans to revive high streets morphed into a chat about his takeaway preferences. Asked for his favourite Greggs order, Burnham replied: “That sausage, bean and cheese thing.”

The PM was referring to what Greggs call their sausage, bean and cheese melt. He may not have known its proper name, but Greggs aren’t daft, and they can spot a marketing opportunity when they see one. Here is the signage that has been on display today at the Greggs near Burnham’s No 10 North office in Manchester.

According to Greggs, sales of the snack at the store have doubled.

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has said that she has told NHS England to start planning ahead for summer heatwaves, just as it prepares every year for a crisis in the winter.

In an article published in the Mirror, Cooper says global heating means Britain will face heatwaves like the one we are going through now “with increasing frequency and increasing intensity”. And this puts extra pressure on the NHS, she says, referencing a report that said there were almost 3,000 excess deaths because of the heat in May and June.

Cooper, who is attending the meeting of the Cobra emergency committee this afternoon to discuss the extreme heat, says:

double quotation markDuring the heatwaves in May and June, we saw more than 2,800 lives lost because of the extreme heat, and this year is on track to see the highest ever number of heat-related deaths. My thoughts go out to every family who has lost loved ones …

Our NHS is used to gearing up for these kinds of pressures in winter. But we are going to need the same level of preparation in future summers. I have told the NHS to start drawing up summer plans now in the way they have traditionally done for winter.

Especially as all the same people who are most at risk when it is very cold are at risk in the extreme heat: older people, the youngest children, and people with existing conditions …

We know Britain will face heatwaves like this with increasing frequency and increasing intensity. So we have to take the health consequences much more seriously, so that everyone is ready when they come.

Cooper also says in her article that some of the £6.75bn being spent on improving NHS buildings will fund air conditioning.

Richard Tice has been accused by Labour’s Bridget Phillipson of mounting a “deeply chilling attempt to silence the free press” after he sent a legal threat to the Guardian over its reporting on his financial affairs, Rowena Mason reports.

Jess Phillips, who was minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls (VAWG) in Keir Starmer’s government, has said that people who commit VAWG should be treated “like terrorists”. She was speaking in an interview on the World at One after the sentencing of Simon Levy, the sexual predator who was able to kill two women because of mistakes made by the police and prosecutors.

double quotation markViolence against women and girls has to be an absolute priority in every single police force in our country. Twenty per cent of callouts to almost every single force in our country is violence against women and girls … it kills way more people on the streets, just in London, let alone anywhere else.

These people are a danger and a risk to our society, and they have to be treated like terrorists, because that is what they are doing. They are harming and killing people on our streets. It’s exactly the same, and it needs to be treated with that level of seriousness.

Sharon Graham has, as expected, been re-elected as general secretary of the Unite union. She faced a leadership challenge from Simon Dubbins, international director at the union, which is the second biggest in the UK and a key player in Labour party politics.

Graham won with 69% of the vote. As usual for an internal union election, turnout was low. Unite has more than 1m members, and only 100,089 people voted.

double quotation markIt’s an honour to be re-elected by Unite members to serve as their general secretary. This decisive victory is a powerful mandate to continue change …

My second period of office will continue to be marked by a relentless focus on the jobs, pay and conditions of workers. It will always be members over ministers and the workplace over Westminster.

We will continue to deliver much needed reform to our union. It is my mission to build the industrial and political power required to better serve the working class.

As Matthew Taylor explained in an article about the election earlier in the summer, Dubbins’ campaign was in part motivated by a concern that, under Graham, Unite has not done enough to counter the threat to the left posed by Reform UK.

Dubbins explained why he was standing against Graham at length last month in this Counterfire interview.

UPDATE: Unite is not giving the turnout figure in the election, but sources say it is around 10%. The journalist Andy Twelves says the figure is 10.31%.

In an interview with Times Radio, Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, claimed that Andy Burnham has had more small boat arrivals in his first three weeks in office than any other prime minister. Philp said:

double quotation markThree thousand have entered our country in the first 22 days of Andy Burnham’s premiership, that is more … than any other prime minister has seen in their first 22 days.

The Press Association’s QuickCheck team have been looking at this – and they say Philp is wrong.

double quotation markBurnham’s first 22 days saw considerably fewer migrants cross the English Channel than the first 22 days of the premierships of Rishi Sunak and Liz Truss.

Government data shows 3,003 people crossed on small boats between July 20 when Burnham became prime minister and August 10, 22 days later.

In the first 22 days of Keir Starmer’s premiership, 2,258 people crossed the English Channel on small boats. In Sunak’s first 22 days, 4,105 people crossed, and the figure for the first 22 days of Liz Truss’s premiership was 4,739.

During Boris Johnson’s first 22 days in office, 138 people were recorded crossing the Channel.

Data collection on small boat crossings started in January 2018 so the figures do not include any other prime minister’s first 22 days.

Boat crossings are very seasonal, meaning prime ministers who enter the role in peak season are likely to see higher crossings in their first few weeks.

Between 2018 and 2025, the months that saw the most crossings were September (28,734 people), August (26,591), July (20,672), and October (20,324).

Starmer, Burnham and Johnson all became prime minister during July. Sunak became prime minister in late October and Truss took the role in early September.

Officials in the Ministry of Justice are reportedly unhappy about the way that, after Andy Burnham announced a new version of the prisoner early release scheme at the start of last week, they have now been asked to revise it again.

double quotation markThere is said to be anger within the Ministry of Justice, where some officials feel they have been unfairly blamed for simply doing their jobs in spelling out the pros and cons of each policy option to the prime minister.

One government source claimed that Burnham appeared to be “trying to be nice to everyone” and failing to understand the trade-offs involved.

“The Ministry of Justice is totally demoralised,” they said. “They never said anything was impossible — they simply spelt out the risks involved.”

And at the Telegraph Will Bolton and Tony Diver have also been talking to an MoJ source (who may or may not be the same one as Swinford’s). They report:
