double quotation markOne senior Ministry of Justice source said: “Alex [Norris, the justice secretary] has 100 per cent been thrown under the bus. There’s a lot of anger and frustration from MoJ to the PM and No 10.”

A senior Labour source added: “There is frustration in the MoJ that he has raised victims’ expectations. If it’s an issue he’s staked himself on, then No 10 should be gripping it. They’re passing it on to Alex Norris, and he’s only been in post for two weeks.”

Swinford says Norris was all set to head off for a summer holiday on Monday night when he was told that Burnham wanted him to find a new early prisoner release mechanism that would keep the killers of PC Andrew Harper in jail.

Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, according to a report by Verdant, a Green thinktank.

The report is here, and here is Heather Stewart’s write-up.

double quotation markSuccessive heatwaves from May to the end of July 2026 have an estimated economic cost of at least £4.4bn. Previous estimates by Verdant placed the cost of the June 2026 heatwave alone at £2.36bn; this figure now includes all three heatwaves this year, from May to the end of July. May’s relatively minor event cost around £500m; July’s larger hit was £1.5bn, over two distinct peaks.

These losses are the result of reduced productivity due to the well-documented effect of all work becoming harder at higher temperatures, and that infrastructure and equipment overheat and fail. For each one degree Celsius temperature increase above 30 degrees in Europe, a 3% reduction in average output per hour has been observed. In a prolonged heatwave, these impacts add up to become significant economic losses. This is only the direct economic cost from productivity losses, and excludes things like losses from wildfires, or higher costs of energy for businesses and households.

Commenting on the report, Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, said it showed why the government needed to “set out an emergency response to the danger facing us now, and the damage coming fast down the tracks as heatwaves and flooding get more extreme”.

John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, was “irresponsible” when he asked Andy Burnham to lift a ban on a Chinese firm building a wind turbine factory in the Highlands, a UK government minister has said.

As the Press Association reports, energy security minister Michael Shanks described the call from John Swinney in support of the proposed Ming Yang facility at Ardersier, near Inverness, as “surprising”.

With the development having the potential to create up to 1,500 jobs in the area, Swinney reportedly asked Burnham to review the government’s decision to block the Chinese investment. The Scotsman reported the SNP leader raised the issue in his first meeting with Burnham, and has also written to the PM on the issue – with Ming Yang also said to have been in contact with the UK Government following the change in leadership.

In April, Swinney described the government’s decision as “anti-Scottish”.

In an interview on BBC Radio Scotland this morning, Shanks said that, after Swinney made those comments earlier this year, he arranged for the first minister to have a “security briefing at the highest level” on the issue.

double quotation markI do think it is surprising he is now making what feels like a political intervention.

I think it is for him to answer why he is balancing what seems to be a political intervention against the country’s national security.

I think it is irresponsible for the first minister to do that.

There is no inherent reason why the UK government would not want to see jobs created in the north of Scotland either, so I hope people would take it on face value when I say there are national security implications. That is a legitimate reason for us to say no to a particular investment.

title: What’s behind Sydney airport’s heavy delays and near-miss incident?
excerpt:
Air traffic controllers are short-staffed and exhausted – and new recruits face a difficult aptitude test and must train in Melbourne

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Trav...
body_text:
Air traffic controllers are short-staffed and exhausted – and new recruits face a difficult aptitude test and must train in Melbourne

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Travellers flying in and out of Sydney airport had already been dealing with heavy delays even before a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac early on Sunday.

The day before, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed as the airport grappled with a lack of air traffic controllers, highlighting how just how delicate the rostering situation is.

While Sunday’s incident is under investigation – an air traffic controller and a tug driver were temporarily stood down for mandatory drug and alcohol testing – the issue has shone a spotlight on the severe staffing shortages of those in charge of managing air traffic, and takeoffs and landings.

While air traffic controllers are entitled to unlimited sick leave under their terms of employment, Scott Nugent, the president of the air traffic controllers’ union Civil Air, says the issue “is that we do not have enough controllers just to fill the base roster before we have any sick leave at all”.

“In practice, the only way you fill the roster is with overtime, and it relies on overtime just to do business as usual,” says Nugent.

The experienced air traffic controller says workers are getting to the point where they’ve done so much overtime that they’re exhausted. Some staff are working 10 days on and then having one day off.

“The reason you’ve seen these delays in the last week is because we increased the spacing between aircraft to maintain safety when we have less people,” he says.

“If you’re doing the work of two people, you can only take half as many planes.”

Much of the problem is tied to a pandemic-era program that incentivised a significant number of experienced staff to leave Airservices Australia, the commonwealth-owned organisation responsible for the management of the country’s skies, in 2021.

With most planes grounded due to pandemic restrictions, 140 employees aged 56 or older accepted a redundancy.

Soon after, the organisation embarked on a large recruitment drive but hirings have failed to keep up with demand.

Despite the starting salary for a qualified air traffic controller post-training being $116,990 a year – an experienced supervisor can earn a base salary of almost $300,000 – Airservices has struggled with recruitment ever since the pandemic.

In February 2024, two air traffic controllers who didn’t show up for work at Sydney airport caused cascading flight delays and cancellations across the country. Airservices narrowly avoided a similar incident in September last year.

At the same time it has been trying to plug roster gaps, Airservices has been preparing for a once-in-a-generation transformation to a new flight-tracking computer system, as well as managing past allegations of workplace bullying.

A review into workplace culture, conducted by the former sex discrimination commissioner Elizabeth Broderick’s firm, found 27% of staff in 2023 had experienced bullying in the past 12 months, up from 23% in 2020.

From July 2022 to 2026, Airservices says it endorsed 245 controllers, most of whom qualified in 2025-2026. Over the same four-year period, 86 controllers left the organisation.

Airservices says it now has a record number of controllers across Australia. There were 985 controllers in December 2020 and 1,073 as of July this year, according to the organisation.

However, the organisation says the demands on its workforce have also grown significantly, citing the new Western Sydney airport and its recent takeover of the airspace at Ballina in northern New South Wales.

There still aren’t enough controllers at Sydney, Australia’s busiest airport.

A newly qualified controller can’t just fill the gap left by a retiring veteran.

After 18 months of training, a newly qualified controller may be able to work in one position at a Sydney tower, such as helping organise the taxiways around the domestic airport.

That person wouldn’t be qualified, for example, to work on the taxiways around the international airport, or runways, which require additional training, making newer employees less able to fill urgent vacancies.

Airservices acknowledges there’s a problem. It says training experienced controllers for Sydney airport is its “top priority” but it can’t say when it will have recruited a sufficient number.

It takes about two years to train a controller, and that’s only if someone can get past the initial screening, which includes a difficult online aptitude test as one of the first hurdles.

“Only a very, very small number of people get through the application process,” says Nugent. “We’re usually talking about 2,000 people who might apply, and you hire 15 of them.”

Additionally, applicants must move to Melbourne for the mandatory training. Only offering training at one location is seen as an impediment, because some applicants don’t want to relocate given there’s a risk they don’t pass.

Airservices says it is considering different training locations, and says it has a new simulator in Sydney.

title: ABC changing editorial policy after Rinehart furore prompts concerns of overreach from academics and advocates
excerpt:
Managing director says guidelines will ensure no individual will ‘be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news p...
body_text:
Managing director says guidelines will ensure no individual will ‘be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A pledge by the ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, to change editorial guidelines on satire and violence after the broadcaster aired a program featuring offensive comments about Gina Rinehart, has sparked concerns about overreach.

The four-minute film, titled A Very Relaxing Video, ran on documentary-reality show Race Around the World on 12 July and sparked a furore over comments made about the billionaire.

The segment concluded with the film-maker, Kate McGuinness, stating: “When the revolution comes will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butthole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing?”

After sustained backlash in News Corp and The West Australian, and threats of legal action from Rinehart, Marks issued an apology last Thursday.

He said while the ombudsman, Fiona Cameron, had found that the film didn’t breach editorial policies on harm and offence, it fell short of “community expectations”, and the ABC would change its editorial guidance.

On ABC Radio North Queensland last Thursday, he said the ABC’s guidelines will now demand that “no individual should be the subject of comedy that is violent in its description in our programming”.

“And I think the ABC has to hold itself to a higher standard and I think it’s really important we make that change.”

Journalist and professor of communication at Deakin University, Matthew Ricketson, said it was poor satire but once McGuinness had apologised for the joke, as she did on 30 July, that should have been “the end of it”.

“It’s a very ill-advised move,” he said of the promised change. “It’s virtually unenforceable … and it’s literally throwing fuel on to the News Corp fire. They will bank that and they will move straight on to the next demand which will be a curtailing if not the abolition of the ABC.”

The ombudsman initially received eight complaints about the program in the week after was broadcast. A further 988 complaints were made after criticism from “several media outlets”, it said in its report.

News Corp’s major mastheads have published 46 articles critiquing the program since it aired, and The West Australian has published 15.

The ombudsman found “a reasonable audience member would be likely to understand the remarks as part of a satirical and exaggerated commentary” rather than encouragement of violence.

The former editorial director of the ABC, Alan Sunderland, agreed with the ombudsman’s findings, which didn’t discount that the joke was in “poor taste”.

He said he wasn’t “perturbed” by the ABC reviewing its guidance, which could help program makers interpret editorial principles if it wasn’t enforceable. But he said “if it’s more elaborate than that then you start to get into problems”.

“You wouldn’t be able to put much [satire] to air,” he said, pointing to Aunty Jack in the 1970s, who threatened to “rip yer bloody arms off” if viewers didn’t watch the next week.

Sunderland said it was a “repeated pattern” to see ABC content picked up and “amplified” by some media and politicians, thereby giving it a “second life”. “Broadcasters can and do apologise without the world coming to an end,” he said.

Journalist, author and academic, Dr Margaret Simons, said Marks was right to apologise but rewriting editorial policies “wasn’t necessary”.

“The problem here is that either somebody didn’t make a judgment call or they made the wrong one,” she said. “I would have thought it was self-evident that a threat of violence, even a satirical threat, is a pretty serious matter.”

Simons said the ABC’s editorial policies required carefully judged decisions, and explicitly stated that contentious decisions should be upwardly referred to an appropriate level.

“My main question is, were the ABC policies followed in the sense of upward referral? Did anybody actually stop to look at this before it was broadcast?” she said.

“If it wasn’t … that in itself is arguably a breach of editorial policy. If editorial policies are substantially rewritten in the light of what I suspect is a failure of the ABC’s internal processes … that’s not good.”

An ABC spokesperson confirmed the changes would be amended “soon”, with approval by the ABC board. It didn’t respond to questions on whether the program had been upwardly referred.

On Saturday, Hancock Prospecting said it would “wait to see long overdue changes to the ABC’s ‘editorial standards’” and accused it of normalising “violent torture against a woman till death”.

“Satire needs to be funny, what the ABC approved to be aired for 25 days, in its violent torture until death content, was not,” it said. “We await a detailed account in relation to who approved this unacceptable piece to be aired, and who approved the long delay in its removal. The buck stops with the heads of the ABC.”

The president of ABC Friends, Cassandra Parkinson, said the ABC had “overreacted in trying to appease Ms Rinehart”.

“I can understand that the ABC issued an apology to avoid a costly legal action, but it’s difficult to understand the rationale for this new rule,” she said.

“Regardless of our views about the ‘joke’ in question, it’s important that the process that follows involves close scrutiny. It’s essential that the ABC hold firm against this sort of external pressure and that it uphold the independence laid out in its charter.”

McGuinness has also apologised over the segment, saying it wasn’t her intention to promote violence.

“My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone. Its purpose was never to be taken literally,” she said in a statement uploaded to the ABC’s website.

title: Victorian police investigate allegation a car drove deliberately at speed towards anti-racism protester
excerpt:
Exclusive: ‘Peaceful community rally’ of more than 150 people was walking in Broadmeadows when car travelling in same direction allegedly approached

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily new...
body_text:
Exclusive: ‘Peaceful community rally’ of more than 150 people was walking in Broadmeadows when car travelling in same direction allegedly approached

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victorian police are investigating allegations that a car was deliberately driven at speed towards a protester taking part in an anti-racism rally in Melbourne last month.

More than 150 people gathered in the outer-north suburb of Broadmeadows on 25 July for what organisers described as a “peaceful community rally”.

After speeches, the group marched to Broadmeadows Town Park, occupying one lane of Tanderrum Drive, a two-lane road.

While the group was walking on the road, a car travelling in the same directionsounded its horn.

Protesters alleged that as the car approached the group, a passenger flung open the door twice, as if trying to push people out of the way.

Video of the incident, seen by Guardian Australia, shows a protester walking on the edge of the group in the lane where the car was attempting to pass. The video shows him turning as the car approaches and appearing to kick at it.

The car then clips the man on the legs and accelerates away.

Witnesses said it did not slow down as it attempted to pass the group.

The protester, who asked not to be identified, alleged that he heard an occupant of the car shout racial abuse before the car struck him.

The comments were not audible in the video, but Guardian Australia spoke to two others at the march who claim to have heard the alleged remarks. Several participants, including the man in the video, said they separately reported the incident directly to police within hours and in the following days.

“It felt surreal. I did not have the chance to even feel anything but shock,” the 43-year-old said.

Merri-bek Socialist Alliance councillor Sue Bolton, an organiser of the event, said the incident contradicted the rally’s purpose, which was to support community members who were “feeling really intimidated” by a recent rise in anti-immigration rhetoric.

Bolton said the group had been in contact with police in the days before the event to make them aware of the rally and received confirmation over the phone that officers would attend, but none did so.

Athiya Zameer, the member of the group designated to liaise with police, said she believed the incident would not have occurred if police had been present.

In a formal complaint to police on behalf of the group, Zameer called for action against the driver, claiming the alleged incident had caused trauma to the person hit by the car, children present and the wider community.

“We want to make sure that people feel safe to do these actions, to raise their voices,” she said. “We live in a community [of people from] migrant backgrounds who are already traumatised by wars and the police … and to have an incident like that just traumatises them even more … that’s really unfortunate.”

In a response to the complaint, seen by Guardian Australia, police confirmed they had been aware of the planned event. The response said the incident was “being actively investigated” and police were “committed to ensuring that allegations are thoroughly assessed”.

They declined to answer questions from Guardian Australia about why officers did not attend the protest.

The Greens state MP Anasina Gray-Barberio, who attended the rally but did not witness the car incident, said “the community expects an urgent and robust response”.

“The community deserves answers … Communities of colour deserve to know that when they’re subjected to violence or racism, those incidents will be treated with the seriousness they deserve,” she said.

title: Heroic Florida K-9 returns to sheriff's office days after being shot protecting 3 deputies, losing leg
excerpt: K-9 Ace returned to the Polk County Sheriff's Office for the first time since surviving a line-of-duty shooting and losing his left front leg as the longtime police dog prepares for retirement. (Polk ...
body_text:
K-9 Ace returned to the Polk County Sheriff's Office for the first time since surviving a line-of-duty shooting and losing his left front leg as the longtime police dog prepares for retirement. (Polk County Sheriff's Office via Facebook)

Less than a week after being shot and losing a leg while protecting three deputies, heroic Florida K-9 Ace was back on his feet Tuesday for an emotional return to the sheriff's office.

Ace, a 7-year-old German shepherd who has served with the Polk County Sheriff's Office since March 2020, was wounded as deputies attempted to arrest 27-year-old Angel Bowers.

Authorities said Bowers allegedly fired at least four rounds at three deputies who were attempting to arrest him after he failed to appear in court. Bowers was killed by deputies at the scene.

DEPUTY US MARSHAL FATALLY SHOT WHILE SERVING ARREST WARRANT IN LOUISIANA

Polk County Sheriff's Office K-9 Ace returned to the agency less than a week after being shot while protecting three deputies and undergoing surgery to amputate his left front leg. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said Ace protected the three deputies from Bowers but was shot in his left front leg, shattering the bone and tearing an artery that caused massive blood loss.

Ace's partner and handler, Deputy Natalie Oestreich, treated his wounds and carried him to safety, according to the sheriff's office.

Ace was rushed to Parkway Veterinary Emergency Clinic in Lakeland, where he was stabilized before a Tampa General Hospital Aeromed helicopter transported him to the Veterinary Medical Center at Lakewood Ranch. Veterinarians there performed a several-hour surgery to amputate his left front leg.

On Sunday, the sheriff's office posted video showing deputies arriving at the veterinary medical center to greet an energetic Ace as he prepared to return home.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND

"Upon waking from the anesthesia, Ace attempted to walk out of there," the sheriff's office wrote. "He has not been deterred since. In fact he outran the camera attempting to film his release this afternoon!"

Video shows Ace interacting with deputies before walking out of the medical center under his own power to thunderous applause while wearing a shirt that read "ride or die."

Two days later, Ace made his first trip back to the sheriff's office since being shot in the line of duty.

"Look at Ace. He's happy; he's eating; he bit my finger," Judd said. "We are so proud of Natalie and Ace. They stood in the gap between good and evil and they saved three deputies' lives. That's why we're so proud of him. He did so good."

MAN WANTED IN DEPUTY AMBUSH CAUGHT AFTER WILDLIFE CAMERA SIGHTING AND MAJOR MANHUNT

K-9 Ace was back on his feet days after suffering a gunshot wound that resulted in the amputation of his left front leg. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)

Judd said Oestreich will spend time with Ace as he continues to recover before she returns to work. Ace, however, will retire from law enforcement.

"Chill out and enjoy your retirement Ace," Judd said.

The sheriff's office also honored Ace in a social media post, writing, "His days of chasing bad guys may be over, but Ace will always be one of our heroes!"

K-9 Ace will retire after being critically wounded while protecting three Polk County deputies during an attempted arrest. (Polk County Sheriff's Office)

Polk Sheriff's Charities Inc. has established a K-9 fund to help support Ace's care. The sheriff's office said those interested in helping can donate directly to the fund through the organization's website.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: All-British chocolate bar made by scientists using Reading-grown cocoa
excerpt:
Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight affect of climate crisis on cocoa plants

The late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate ...
body_text:
Master’s student made first bar with 100% UK ingredients since 1932 to highlight affect of climate crisis on cocoa plants

The late queen was the only person in history to have ever eaten a chocolate bar made with 100% British ingredients, after she was given one as a six-year-old in 1932 by the confectioner Rowntree’s.

The bar was created from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant, at Rowntree’s headquarters in York.

But now, others could have the same experience after scientists at the University of Reading created a bar with cocoa beans grown in Berkshire.

The bar was crafted to celebrate the university’s 100th anniversary, made with cocoa grown from plants in the institute’s collection.

The UK makes some of the world’s best chocolate in a market worth £10.4bn, but the industry is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.

Maha Khan, a master’s student at the university, decided to make a bar with cocoa from Reading. She harvested, fermented, and processed the beans at the university’s food department.

She said: “It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading.

“This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate change is already causing problems in countries that produce most of the world’s cocoa. Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate.

“I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world.”

She said the chocolate is “delicious”, adding that it had a very rich flavour: “It’s incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here. It was also really interesting to taste the raw cacao before it gets processed – the beans are coated in a white flesh that tastes like lychee and isn’t something many people in this country get to try.”

As well as being somewhat of a stunt, the university hopes that this can highlight the importance of its work in preserving different varieties of cocoa, which could be resistant to changes in weather brought by climate breakdown, as well as pests and diseases made more common by a heating planet.

Reading has more than 300 types of cocoa plant at its international cocoa quarantine centre, which handles 97% of the world’s international movement of cocoa plants.

Chocolate prices have risen in recent years as high temperatures in regions where cocoa is grown have stunted the growth of plants. Extreme rainfall made more likely by climate breakdown has also drowned crops across Africa.

The bar is currently a limited edition, with only six made so far, but Khan said there are hopes to ramp up production, depending on the availability of the beans – a single cocoa pod can take six months to grow.

She hopes to give one to the Princess of Wales: “We haven’t decided yet who will get to eat the chocolate. As the last British chocolate made was eaten by the future queen in 1932, it would be fitting if the next bar was a gift to another future queen, the Princess of Wales, who, like the chocolate, was also born in Reading.”

title: Israeli raids, demolitions continue as UN warns West Bank at breaking point
excerpt: Israeli forces have continued their crackdown in the occupied West Bank, arresting at least 23 Palestinians and demolishing several homes, as the United Nations warned that the situation in the territ...
body_text:
Israeli forces have continued their crackdown in the occupied West Bank, arresting at least 23 Palestinians and demolishing several homes, as the United Nations warned that the situation in the territory was at a “breaking point”.

The arrests and demolitions on Tuesday came as dozens of Israeli settlers continued raids on Palestinian villages, including one in Khirbet ar-Ras al-Ahmar, where a water pipeline was destroyed.

According to the Palestinian Wafa news agency, those detained included two children, one of whom had a disability, as well as a man who was taken while he was grazing his livestock in al-Hadidiyah in the northern Jordan Valley.

At least 11 others were arrested in the Jenin governorate, while five were detained in the Bethlehem area.

In the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, Israeli forces demolished the family home of Farouq Ramadan, one of four Palestinians killed during a confrontation with Israeli settlers on July 24. Two Israelis were also killed in the incident.

Israel maintains a policy of demolishing the homes belonging to relatives of Palestinians involved in attacks against Israelis, an approach human rights groups have condemned as collective punishment.

Near Yatta in the Hebron governorate, Israeli forces also demolished the home of Ibrahim Mifleh al-Atimin and filled in a water well, displacing nine members of his family, according to Wafa.

Israeli soldiers demolished 12 commercial warehouses in the village of Anza and bulldozed an agricultural facility in Yarza, east of Tubas. In Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, they issued demolition notices for the Khallat al-Dabaa school, as well as several homes and agricultural structures.

According to UN figures, Israel has demolished an average of 122 Palestinian buildings every month this year.

Separately, dozens of settlers attacked a group of Palestinians ploughing their lands in Al-Mughayyir, wounding six people, including three children and two women.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Al-Mughayyir, said the settlers also burned part of the valley and attacked nearby homes.

“Upwards of 60 percent of Al-Mughayyir’s land has been confiscated by the Israeli army, while Israeli settlers have set up at least 11 illegal outposts in the village, barring the farmers from their land,” she said.

“Some 119 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been uprooted by this very dynamic in the past three years. Palestinians are treated as trespassers in their own land, while Israeli settlers slash, burn, and steal the land with impunity,” she added.

In Burqa, northwest of Nablus, six Palestinians, including two children, were wounded after Israeli forces assaulted residents during a raid, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent. Settlers also raided the Nablus-area villages of Awarta, Osarin and Sarra.

The attacks form part of a sharp escalation in violence by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank as Israel gears up for a parliamentary election in October.

Addressing the UN Security Council on Tuesday, Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov said the West Bank was at “breaking point”.

He said Israeli forces and settlers have killed 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, in the occupied West Bank so far this year, while about 3,800 Palestinians – nearly half of them children – have been displaced by settler violence, demolitions and evictions.

The UN has documented more than 1,430 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across roughly 260 Palestinian communities in 2026, many carried out in the presence of Israeli forces, Alakbarov said. Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities have been fully or partially displaced, including 47 completely uprooted, affecting more than 6,390 people.

Alakbarov said settler attacks, once concentrated mainly in Area C, where Israel holds full civil and security control, are increasingly spreading into Areas A and B.

Israeli authorities have also advanced or approved roughly 12,360 settlement housing units across the West Bank this year, including 5,160 in occupied East Jerusalem, he said.

“These are interconnected steps, not isolated developments,” Alakbarov said, warning that they were reshaping the occupied West Bank, weakening Palestinian governance and advancing “de facto annexation”.

title: Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China
excerpt:
Forecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hours

Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landsl...
body_text:
Forecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hours

Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China.

Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.

Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.

Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.

The rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.

Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.

The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.

In the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas.

Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports.

China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive ‌weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the ​emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons.

Rainfall records have also been broken elsewhere in central China. Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media.

title: Massive bailout for Australia’s largest aluminium smelter expected to be announced by PM and NSW premier
excerpt:
Rio Tinto said in December it may cease operations at the Tomago aluminium smelter at the end of its current electricity supply contract

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get ou...
body_text:
Rio Tinto said in December it may cease operations at the Tomago aluminium smelter at the end of its current electricity supply contract

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese and the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, are preparing to mount a major bailout of Australia’s largest aluminium smelter, in a deal worth as much as $2.5bn.

Resources giant Rio Tinto said in December it was contemplating ceasing operations at the Tomago aluminium smelter in NSW at the end of its current electricity supply contract.

The site accounts for more than 10% of energy use in the state and employs about 1,000 workers.

Albanese and Minns were expected to visit Tomago, located north-west of Newcastle, on Thursday morning to announce a joint federal-NSW funding injection, which would come as rising energy costs put the site’s immediate viability in doubt.

Guardian Australia has been told the looming deal is worth $2.5bn over 10 years, with as much as $1bn in capital improvements expected from the site’s owners.

Multiple sources confirmed the announcement was due to take place on Thursday morning, with the costs split 50-50 between the federal government and NSW.

The Australian Financial Review first reported the looming announcement on Wednesday, linking the deal to power purchase agreements with the government-owned utility Snowy Hydro.

Guardian has been told the deal will create about 2.5GW of new energy supply.

The government also offered $600m to keep Glencore’s copper smelter and refinery in Mt Isa operating, as well as $240m for smelters in Hobart and Port Pirie.

The bailout comes as a number of smelters prepare to switch to 100% renewable energy in the coming decade. Tomago had announced in 2021 it would “for all intents and purposes” be 100% renewable by the end of the decade.

Federal Labor has offered a growing list of taxpayer-funded bailout packages to help metal processors around the country. Promises of $2bn for Rio Tinto’s Boyne smelter in Queensland and $2.4bn for the Whyalla steelworks in South Australia have attracted criticism.

The industry minister, Tim Ayres, has been involved in the negotiations and is expected to join the announcement with Albanese and Minns. Ayres has previously highlighted “a very tough and volatile global trading environment” for trade in aluminium, for reasons including the “over-subsidisation in some markets, tariff responses in others”.

Albanese in December forecast a deal to provide Tomago with clean power and keep the site operational.

“If Australia doesn’t produce aluminium, then the knock-on effect in other industries is significant because aluminium is increasingly a vital product,” the prime minister said at the time.

Asked about Tomago on Tuesday, the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, warned it would not be “sustainable for our country to have to expect massive industries to live government blank cheque to government to blank cheque”.

Stressing he did not want workers in the Hunter region to lose their jobs due to tough economic conditions, Canavan said businesses needed to have a sustainable economic footing, calling for the scrapping of net zero by 2050 policies.

Tomago produces up to 590,000 tonnes a year of aluminium, used in the manufacture of a wide range of products including consumer and industrial packaging, construction materials, solar panels and wind turbines.

title: Francesca Hong aims to ride progressive wave in Wisconsin primary for governor
excerpt:
Democratic socialist is frontrunner in four-way race to face Republican Tom Tiffany in test of anti-establishment mood

Wisconsin voters will decide on Tuesday whether to nominate a democratic sociali...
body_text:
Democratic socialist is frontrunner in four-way race to face Republican Tom Tiffany in test of anti-establishment mood

Wisconsin voters will decide on Tuesday whether to nominate a democratic socialist for the state’s highest office in the latest test of an anti-establishment wave among Democratic primary voters.

Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist state lawmaker, emerged as the frontrunner in a four-way race to succeed Tony Evers, the Democratic governor who is not seeking another term.

Evers threw his support behind David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive. Crowley previously left the race, before re-entering it on 18 July.

Crowley and Evers toured the state in the last two weeks, centering his campaign around electability, saying Crowley was more poised to win a general election in a swing state like Wisconsin than Hong.

Eyes turned to the Wisconsin governor’s race after Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in Michigan last week in the most recent example of a progressive beating out a moderate. Nextdoor, Minnesota voters have also been weighing a US Senate primary between a moderate and a progressive.

After a wave of wins of progressives and democratic socialists in solidly blue parts of the country, the midwest primaries centered more on electability concerns given the close nature of statewide races there.

While some saw Crowley’s re-entry as evidence that the establishment was working to derail Hong’s campaign, Crowley balked at the idea that he was part of the establishment.

Hong, meanwhile, saw her past comments – including a tweet that suggested cancelling Thanksgiving, and previous support for defunding the police – scrutinized by journalists and attacked by Republicans, led by Donald Trump, as more national attention turned to Wisconsin’s primary.

Marquette University Law School surveyed the Democratic primary in late July, after Crowley re-entered, and found Hong leading the pack, though a sizable chunk of voters were still undecided at that time.

The race had rearranged itself multiple times in the weeks leading up to 11 August, landing at four candidates: Hong, Crowley, the state senator Kelda Roys, and the former state administration department head Joel Brennan. A previous top contender, Sara Rodriguez, left the race following campaign finance irregularities, after which Crowley re-entered the race. Mandela Barnes, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in 2022, dropped out on 31 July.

Hong, a chef and former restaurant owner from Madison, was first elected to the state assembly in 2020. She ran on a platform that included childcare for all, free school meals and a one-year moratorium on new datacenter construction. She said voters throughout the state have pushed back against the political establishment and want candidates who will advocate for changes that materially improve their lives.

“I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she previously told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.”

The winner will face Tom Tiffany, a Republican congressman and ardent Trump supporter who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. He voted against certifying the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost.

Tiffany’s role in the 2020 election highlighted the importance of keeping the governor’s office for Democrats. Democrats also hope to win both chambers of the state legislature to install a governing trifecta and enact their agenda.

Elsewhere in Wisconsin, voters in the western part of the state will decide which Democratic contender will face the Republican Derrick Van Orden in the third congressional district, a key pickup opportunity for Democrats.

Rebecca Cooke, a “blue dog” Democrat who previously ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, has seen national support for her campaign against Emily Berge, a former Eau Claire city council president.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee endorsed Cooke, which angered some local Democrats who saw it as interfering in a primary. Berge’s momentum, amid a wave of anti-establishment sentiment, had other national groups spending to boost Cooke, who they believe is most poised to win the district.

title: Progressive Peggy Flanagan sweeps Minnesota Senate primary in race defined by anti-ICE anger
excerpt:
State’s Democratic lieutenant governor bests Angie Craig in another election contest pitting a progressive against a moderate

Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic prima...
body_text:
State’s Democratic lieutenant governor bests Angie Craig in another election contest pitting a progressive against a moderate

Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s lieutenant governor, won the Democratic primary for US Senate in a race centered on immigration enforcement after the Trump administration crackdown turned deadly and destructive earlier this year.

Flanagan ousted congresswoman Angie Craig in yet another example of progressive campaigns toppling moderates amid an anti-establishment wave among Democrats.

“It’s time to fight for what people actually need,” Flanagan recently told the Guardian. “And so often I think Democrats are like: ‘What do we think we can win?’ Instead of: ‘What are the fights that we should be picking?’”

Flanagan will now face Michele Tafoya, a Republican former National Football League sideline reporter, in November. If she wins, Flanagan will become the first Native American woman in the Senate.

Meanwhile, the state’s gubernatorial race proved a rebuke of Donald Trump’s endorsement power as Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, lost to Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota house speaker. Demuth will face Amy Klobuchar, a Democratic US senator, in November, where Klobuchar is favored to win.

Lindell’s significant campaign liabilities had led his own party to speak out against his campaign. He is contending with ongoing defamation cases because of his election denialism, as well as a potential campaign finance violation for handing out free pillows at a parade. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, which faces legal claims for unpaid bills.

Minnesota leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor and a Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972.

Both the governor and US Senate seats are fully open, with no incumbents seeking to stay in office. Tim Walz, the Democratic governor, initially sought a third term, but dropped his bid after ongoing fraud scandals threatened to distract from the race. Tina Smith, the Democratic US senator, decided not to run again, saying she wanted to spend time with her grandkids and make way for new faces in the chamber. She endorsed Flanagan.

The role of immigration enforcement served as a major issue in Minnesota’s US Senate primary after the state experienced devastation, including the deaths of two residents and hundreds of deportations, when the Trump administration sent in thousands of immigration officers in early 2026 as part of Operation Metro Surge.

The lingering impacts of the crackdown had dogged Craig, who as a congresswoman voted for the Laken Riley Act, a federal law that requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes. In March, Craig said she regretted her vote on the act, but it has followed her campaign throughout her run for Senate.

Craig, meanwhile, attacked Flanagan on fraud scandals that have rocked state social services, saying the lieutenant governor had not faced accountability for any role in the scandals.

Craig, 54, was first elected to Congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide.

Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation who began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins in November.

Flanagan said she expected to be part of the US Senate “fight club” of progressive senators in the chamber. She was boosted by its members, Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders.

“Peggy Flanagan’s win is further proof that the many can beat the money,” Warren said in a statement. “Voters want leaders with backbones who will stand up to dark money super Pacs and fight to make life more affordable. I was the very first senator to endorse Peggy because she’s the fighter we need in Washington.”

In congressional races, Matt Little edged out Matt Klein and Kaela Berg to win the Democratic nod in the purple district now represented by Craig, the second congressional district made up of suburbs and exurbs south of the Twin Cities. Little had patrolled immigration agents during the surge.

In the first congressional district in southern Minnesota, Jake Johnson, a high school teacher, secured the nomination to take on Brad Finstad in a potential Democratic pickup.

And in the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota, reality TV star Luke Gulbranson lost his bid to Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, who will face Republican Pete Stauber in November.

title: STATE OF PLAY: Highly watched Hong race remains too close to call as progressives notch key primary wins
excerpt:
Francesca Hong, the socialist Democratic gubernatorial candidate, speaks with reporters after voting on primary day in Madison, Wisconsin.

A series of closely watched primaries across the Upper Midwe...
body_text:
Francesca Hong, the socialist Democratic gubernatorial candidate, speaks with reporters after voting on primary day in Madison, Wisconsin.

A series of closely watched primaries across the Upper Midwest delivered key victories for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing Tuesday night — with one major test still hanging in the balance in battleground Wisconsin.

Minnesota was among the clearest signs of progressive strength, with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan winning the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Tina Smith, while progressive "Squad" member Rep. Ilhan Omar secured another primary victory in her overwhelmingly blue Minneapolis-area district.

Flanagan defeated Rep. Angie Craig in a closely watched clash between the party’s progressive and establishment wings. Flanagan drew support from prominent figures on the left, while Craig had the backing of several leading establishment Democrats.

SOCIALIST WINNING STREAK FACES MAJOR SWING-STATE TEST AS POLLS CLOSE IN WISCONSIN

The 2026 midterms will determine control of the House and Senate, shaping President Donald Trump's legislative agenda during the final two years of his term. (Al Drago/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, progressive "Squad" member Rep. Ilhan Omar won the Democratic primary in Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, securing another victory for one of the most prominent members of the House’s progressive wing.

Omar’s win adds to a string of primary victories for the congresswoman, who has previously survived well-funded efforts to oust her.

MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call/Getty Images)

But the biggest remaining question of the night is in Wisconsin, where Democratic voters are still waiting to learn who will carry the party’s banner in the race to succeed outgoing Gov. Tony Evers.

State Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, is seeking to extend the progressive left’s string of victories in one of the nation’s most closely divided battleground states, where Democrats are fighting to keep control of the governor’s mansion.

Hong, a 37-year-old former chef and single mother, has drawn backing from nationally known progressives, including Reps. Omar and Ro Khanna of California.

Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, is seeking the Democratic nomination for governor in one of Tuesday night’s most closely watched primaries. (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

She is running on a platform that includes raising Wisconsin’s minimum wage from $7.25 to $20 an hour, guaranteed paid leave and a one-year moratorium on new AI data centers.

Hong has also faced scrutiny over years-old social media posts calling for defunding and abolishing the police, positions she now says she no longer supports.

With most of Tuesday’s marquee contests decided, Wisconsin stands as the night’s biggest remaining test of whether the progressive left can carry its momentum into one of the nation’s premier battleground states.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Five teen friends killed after vehicle plunges down Colorado cliff, leaving community shattered
excerpt: Gwinnett County Police dashcam footage shows a horrific three-vehicle collision on May 23, where a 7-year-old boy was miraculously ejected from a truck onto a police cruiser. Officer Arianna James, wh...
body_text:
Gwinnett County Police dashcam footage shows a horrific three-vehicle collision on May 23, where a 7-year-old boy was miraculously ejected from a truck onto a police cruiser. Officer Arianna James, who witnessed the crash, describes rushing to the child's aid, comforting him as he feared being left by his father. This terrifying event highlights the importance of child safety in vehicles.

Five 17-year-old friends were killed when their vehicle plunged off a cliff and down a steep Colorado hillside, leaving their families and community grappling with an unimaginable loss just as a new school year begins.

The five boys, all from Grand Junction, were traveling along Lookout Lane late Saturday when their vehicle veered off the roadway and went down the steep incline, according to authorities.

Three of the teenagers, including the driver and front-seat passenger, were wearing seat belts, while the other two were not buckled in and were ejected from the vehicle, the Mesa County Coroner's Office said.

SILICON VALLEY DEVELOPER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER INVESTIGATORS SAY TESLA REACHED 142 MPH BEFORE FATAL CRASH

Grand Junction police and fire crews responded near Lookout Lane after a vehicle plunged down a steep hillside, killing five 17-year-old boys. (Grand Junction Police Department)

All five died from injuries sustained in the crash.

Authorities were not alerted to the wreck until approximately 7:45 a.m. Sunday, when 911 dispatchers received a report that a vehicle may have gone over the edge of a cliff, according to the Grand Junction Police Department.

Police and firefighters responding to the area discovered the wrecked vehicle along the hillside.

Speed is being investigated as a possible factor, police said. Authorities have not publicly identified the driver or said what caused the vehicle to leave the roadway.

MISSOURI SKYDIVING PLANE CRASH THAT KILLED ALL 12 ABOARD IS A 'DEVASTATING LOSS,' COMPANY SAYS

First responders work along the steep hillside near Lookout Lane following a crash that killed five 17-year-old boys in Grand Junction, Colorado. (Grand Junction Police Department)

The coroner's office said it would not release the teenagers' names because of its policy against publicly identifying minors.

Though the teens have been identified by families and loved ones as those in the Grand Junction community share memories and rally around those left behind.

One of the victims was Braden Taylor, 17, whose grandfather, Calvin Wilken, confirmed his death in an emotional Facebook post obtained by Fox News Digital.

"Very sad news our youngest grandson Braden 17 died in a car rollover down 5 ledges of a very steep drop off over looking the railroad tracks and the Gunnison River," Wilken wrote.

"He was a passenger with 4 of his buddies, all deceased," he added.

Wilken said the crash occurred just blocks from the family's former home in a ridge-top development above the area.

A GoFundMe established for Braden's parents said the teenager was their youngest son and that the family is now confronting unexpected funeral expenses while trying to process his death.

GEORGIA TEACHER, FATHER HAILED AS HERO AFTER DYING TO SAVE GIRL FROM MYRTLE BEACH RIP CURRENT

William Simms, 17, was killed alongside four friends after their vehicle plunged down a steep hillside in Grand Junction, Colorado. (GoFundMe)

Tristan Tucker, 17, was killed alongside four friends after their vehicle plunged down a steep hillside in Grand Junction, Colorado. (GoFundMe)

Tyler Martinez, 17, was killed alongside four friends after their vehicle plunged down a steep hillside in Grand Junction, Colorado. (Aimee Huffman Facebook)

Titus Gould, 17, was among five teenage boys killed in a vehicle crash off Lookout Lane in Grand Junction, Colorado. (Meal Train)

Braden Taylor, 17, was killed alongside four friends in a vehicle crash off Lookout Lane in Grand Junction, Colorado. (GoFundMe)

"Wade and Michelle are now facing the unimaginable pain of losing their youngest son while also carrying the weight of sudden funeral expenses," the fundraiser said.

The scale of the loss has rippled across Grand Junction.

Modern Classic Motors, a local business, shared verified donation links for all five families and said the tragedy was weighing particularly heavily on the community as students returned to school.

"Our hearts are broken for the five young lives tragically lost over the weekend and for their family and friends who are left with this unimaginable loss," the business wrote on Facebook.

"As the new school year kicks off today, we can only imagine the heaviness and sadness that is being felt throughout our schools today," the post continued.

The four other teenagers were identified by loved ones as Tristan Tucker, Titus Gould, William Simms and Tyler Martinez, according to the Daily Mail.

Tucker had been preparing to begin his senior year of high school, get his driver's license and experience the milestones that come with being 17, according to a fundraiser for his family cited by the outlet.

He was remembered as being "full of life, potential, and a free spirit."

A Meal Train was also established to support Gould's family following his death, according to the Daily Mail.

Martinez's grandmother, Debbie Gallegos Martinez, publicly mourned her grandson after the crash.

Grand Junction police officers investigate the steep hillside near Lookout Lane where five 17-year-old boys were killed after their vehicle left the roadway in Grand Junction, Colorado. (Grand Junction Police Department)

"With a heavy heart and tears rolling down my cheek my grandson was one of this [sic] boys," she wrote, according to the outlet.

Another family member asked people to keep all five families in their prayers, calling the tragedy "devastating and heartbreaking."

The Grand Junction Police Department also issued an emotional message.

"Our hearts are heavy following the tragic losses this weekend," the department wrote. "You're our neighbors, our friends, and our family."

"We grieve alongside our community and stand together to support one another."

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Lindsay Clancy defense wants TikToker to expose hospital ‘lies’ as judge warns ‘this is not Tripadvisor’
excerpt:
Legal teams debate the relevance of a former McLean Hospital employee's potential testimony regarding Lindsay Clancy's treatment options.

A dispute rooted in a TikTok video arose at the outset of Lin...
body_text:
Legal teams debate the relevance of a former McLean Hospital employee's potential testimony regarding Lindsay Clancy's treatment options.

A dispute rooted in a TikTok video arose at the outset of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial Tuesday, as her attorneys moved to add a former mental hospital staff member to the witness list — one who had publicly accused witnesses of spreading "lies and misrepresentations" about the psychiatric facility where Clancy was treated weeks before she killed her three children.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan to add former McLean clinical social worker Emily Thorndike to the witness list, arguing that her years working on the same short-term unit could rebut what he described as a misleading picture of a "five star" hospital overflowing with treatment options that Clancy refused.

"Her involvement in this case came about after one of the prosecutors — I don't recall which — made it out on direct examination that McLean is some kind of a five-star institution where the doctors, the psychiatrists, the psychotherapists, and the counselors were all banging into each other in the hallway trying to interview Miss Clancy, who was just blithely refusing care and treatment, which is not the case," Reddington said.

WATCH: Defense seeks to add former McLean Hospital employee to witness list in Lindsay Clancy case

LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

"So now the jury is left with that image that McLean is purportedly some kind of a five-star hospital because they are affiliated, quote-unquote, with Harvard," he continued.

Clancy is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL

Prosecutors, meanwhile, fired back that Thorndike had left McLean roughly a year before Clancy’s stay, had no firsthand knowledge of her treatment and had been following the trial online before posting her opinions online.

title: UK heatwaves may have cost economy £4.4bn in lost output so far this year, analysis finds
excerpt:
Verdant thinktank says cost could top £25bn a year by 2030 and calls for maximum temperature for working and urban redesign to cool down cities

Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely ...
body_text:
Verdant thinktank says cost could top £25bn a year by 2030 and calls for maximum temperature for working and urban redesign to cool down cities

Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, new analysis shows.

Green thinktank Verdant had suggested June’s unseasonally hot weather had an economic cost of £2.36bn. Updating its assessment to include last month’s high temperatures, it finds a £4.4bn hit to output.

As temperatures soar once again this week, Verdant’s director, James Meadway, said: “The economic costs of climate change are already with us, and set to worsen in future years. Action by the government to protect workers and businesses from the severe effects of extreme heat is well overdue.”

Direct economic costs arise because workers across many industries become less productive in heatwaves, while infrastructure and equipment overheats and has to be shut down.

This week’s amber weather warning for extreme heat in England from the Met Office, comes after three previous heatwaves in the UK in May, June and July. The forecaster has said the UK is on course to record its hottest summer ever.

Verdant is calling for the government to implement a maximum working temperature; and be ready to step in to compensate workers when they are forced to cut their hours because of extreme heat.

The report also points to the need for investment in urban redesign, to create more cooler green spaces in the UK’s towns and cities.

Verdant’s estimates exclude indirect losses such as the cost of fighting wildfires, and additional electricity consumption from running fans and air conditioning. The largest effect is likely to have been felt in London and the south-east, where temperatures have been highest, the thinktank argues.

If heatwaves continue to intensify at the same rate as in the last decade, it suggests the annual economic cost could rise to more than £25bn by 2030.

Verdant relies on cross-European estimates by the insurer Allianz, that suggest for every degree above 30C that temperatures rise, workers’ output an hour declines by 3%.

The estimates correspond with work by the Grantham Research Institute at London School of Economics, which suggested a £1bn-plus loss of output during June’s heatwave alone, from workers cutting back their hours or being less productive than usual, because of high temperatures.

In a survey of 2,000 people, the institute’s researchers found that 3.6% of respondents did not work at all during the week of 22 June due to searing temperatures; while 87% reported at least one health-related impact, from disrupted sleep to dizziness.

Economists have increasingly warned about the mounting economic costs of extreme weather events – including the risks of higher inflation due to rising food prices, as production is hit by droughts, floods and wildfires.

Almost three-quarters of England has been declared officially in drought after the repeated heatwaves, which have also affected much of Europe this summer.

The London mayor, Sadiq Khan, recently pointed to the impact of this year’s extreme temperatures as evidence that Labour should take on net zero sceptics and stick to its climate targets. “The climate emergency is here – and no one can say they didn’t see it coming,” he wrote.

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the TUC, said: “As climate change causes more heatwaves, workers are suffering – and productivity is taking a hit too. Many of us have experienced this directly as we’ve struggled to keep working through the heat.

“Unions are calling for rules that require employers to take action to reduce temperatures when they exceed 24C, and for work to stop when temperatures reach 30C, or 27C for strenuous jobs.”

Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White commanded the spotlight for more than two minutes before Tuesday night’s game. But once the ball went in the air, her team did the rest of the talking.

Fever guard Kelsey Mitchell caught fire early, scoring 20 of her 28 points in the first half, while backcourt running mate Caitlin Clark finished with 22 points and 10 assists as Indiana cruised past the New York Liberty, 106-92, for its seventh win in nine games.

Caitlin Clark (22) of the Indiana Fever shoots the ball during a game against the New York Liberty on Aug. 11, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana. (A.J. Mast/NBAE via Getty Images)

Mitchell made 11 of her 16 attempts from the field and she, like Clark and Sophie Cunningham, made four 3-pointers. Cunningham finished the game with 12 points and Aliyah Boston added 19 points and seven rebounds.

Tyasha Harris, Kelsey Mitchell, Myisha Hines-Allen and Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever look on during a game against the New York Liberty on Aug. 11, 2026, at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana. (A.J. Mast/NBAE via Getty Images)

When Indiana’s 3s stopped falling in the third quarter, New York charged back quickly and cut the deficit to 66-57 with 6:51 to play. The Fever recovered, with Mitchell’s three-point play and Cunningham’s three-pointer in the final minute of the period pushing the lead to 87-67.

Before the game, White defended herself after she was criticized for her response to DiJonai Carrington’s flagrant foul on Cunningham, and pleaded with people to focus on the sport and not the continual sideshows.

We are connected. We will not be divided. Every day these women put their ass on the line. Every day when they go low, we go high. Love will win. Grace will win. Humility will win and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

After making the comments, White immediately left without taking questions.
