title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to what the Senate did and didn’t do overnight
excerpt: Fox News' chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's race to clear a packed agenda before the recess, including President Donald Trump's demand for a vote on the 'Save Amer...
body_text:
Fox News' chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's race to clear a packed agenda before the recess, including President Donald Trump's demand for a vote on the 'Save America Act' amid legislative hurdles.

The Senate wrapped up its summer session at 4:57 a.m. ET.

Senators knocked two major items off their checklist. They confirmed Todd Blanche as the nation’s 88th Attorney General.

They also approved a bipartisan interim spending bill that likely goes a long way toward preventing a government shutdown in October.

But nearly as important as what senators accomplished is what didn’t get done.

The U.S. Capitol Building seen at sunset. (Emma Woodhead/Fox News Digital)

The Senate did not stay in session and attempt to pass the SAVE America Act.

In fact, there was not even procedural stunting by the pro-SAVE America Act Republicans, who advocated blowing up the August recess.

TRUMP PUMPS BRAKES ON SENATE BUDGET PLAN, DELAYING GOP SAVE AMERICA PUSH

Moreover, the Senate did not take a vote on a budget framework which could enable them to eventually tack on some election integrity measures – and pass them at a later date in a bill not subject to a filibuster.

Expect some conservatives to rail against the Senate for not working this out.

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio., speaks at the U.S. Capitol. The Senate blocked his voter ID measure in a test vote ahead of the August recess. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The SAVE America Act continues to lack votes. However, advocates of the bill can use the decision by the Senate to leave town without passing it as an opportunity to apply pressure on its opponents.

That said, the Senate did take a test vote on a more narrow voter ID bill backed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. The Senate blocked that bill.

But the test vote got Democrats on the record for opposing it. And giving Husted a vote on his measure was a tactical move to boost his chances in a competitive race this fall against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio.

The Senate did not take a test vote on the bipartisan bill to regulate money for intercollegiate athletics – despite the endorsement by the Big 10 and SEC.

PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT STALLS IN OVERNIGHT SENATE SHOWDOWN, VOTE PUSHED TO SEPTEMBER AFTER CHAOTIC EVENING

In fact, President Trump even implored the Senate to stay in session in August to pass the bill authored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the panel.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said the Protect College Sports Act will be "one of our first orders of business" in September. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

The legislation was beset by an internecine fight among Republicans about whether the legislation kept men from competing in women’s sports.

The President published a full-throated endorsement of the legislation Friday night, declaring that the measure did go far enough. "Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying," wrote the President on Truth Social.

In an overnight statement, Cruz said that the bill was still in play.

"The good news is that when the Senate returns in September, the Protect College Sports Act will be one of our first orders of business, having locked in a vote," said Cruz.

However, no vote is officially secured on the Senate docket.

But what about a test vote on a bill to regulate cryptocurrency?

It was thought that the Senate might pursue that bill in the closing days of the summer session. But the differences were just too wide to close.

However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up a procedural vote on cryptocurrency for September 15.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: University of Michigan plans to shield 2027 freshman letter grades from transcripts in new mental health plan
excerpt:
‘Fox News Saturday Night’ host Jimmy Failla discusses the University of Michigan's decision to drop letter grades for some 2027 freshmen on ‘America Reports.’

Freshmen at the University of Michigan n...
body_text:
‘Fox News Saturday Night’ host Jimmy Failla discusses the University of Michigan's decision to drop letter grades for some 2027 freshmen on ‘America Reports.’

Freshmen at the University of Michigan next year are set to get a semester-long break from having letter grades appear on their transcripts, as school officials look for new ways to combat the "mental health crisis" affecting higher education.

Starting in fall 2027, incoming first-year students enrolled in the public research university's College of Literature, Science, and the Arts (LSA) will have their first-semester grades designated as pass or no credit on their transcripts in an attempt to "curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," according to the university.

"Our goal is to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys — core elements of a liberal arts and sciences education," the statement continued.

EDUCATION SECRETARY LINDA MCMAHON RIPS CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE ‘COMPROMISE,’ TELLS NEWSOM TO ‘PICK A SIDE’

University of Michigan students walk on the UM campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on April 3, 2025. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

The LSA, which is the largest of the university’s 19 colleges and serves approximately 19,700 undergraduate students, will provide students with their letter grades throughout the semester — but will not include the final average on their transcripts.

Transcripts will instead show a "P" for pass or "NC" for no credit.

The covered grades will not be factored into students' grade point averages, a move university officials say will give first-year students greater freedom to explore academically.

"For example, they can explore a subject that may not come easily to them or take a course in a new field without the fear that a low grade may have long-term consequences," the university added. " LSA is investing in students’ well-being and growth by fostering a culture of connection and collaboration — rather than competition."

HARVARD FACULTY VOTE TO CAP 'A' GRADES AT 20% IN SWEEPING EFFORT TO COMBAT DECADES OF GRADE INFLATION

A University of Michigan flag hangs on the Michigan Union building on the school's campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Monday, July 28, 2025. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under the new policy, university officials will keep students' first-semester letter grades internally for administrative purposes, including academic advising, potential academic awards and scholarships, internship and other professional applications, athletic eligibility, compliance reporting, degree progress and financial aid determinations.

Additionally, the 2027 policy only applies to incoming freshmen enrolled in the LSA, with school officials adding there is no opt-out option.

"An opt-in structure would defeat the purpose of facilitating students’ transition to campus, supporting mental health and well-being, and bolstering intrinsic motivations for learning," the university said.

Michigan is now the latest in a small group of schools throughout the country that have chosen to enact similar policies, including Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College and the California Institute of Technology.

CALIFORNIA PROFESSOR ARGUES NEED FOR 'OBJECTIVE MEASURES' AFTER STATE DROPS ACT/SAT REQUIREMENT

A student walks through the University of Michigan campus in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Monday, July 28, 2025. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While the program is aimed at supporting students’ mental health, psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert believes it runs the risk of doing more harm than good.

"We’re raising a generation of students to believe that discomfort is dangerous," Alpert, author of "Therapy Nation," told Fox News Digital. "It isn’t. A bad grade can be upsetting, embarrassing and stressful. That’s not a mental health emergency. That’s college."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alpert went on to add that while the policy was created to relieve students of the pressure and stress from the first semester of college, it could actually risk harming their preparedness for life outside of the learning environment.

"This is therapy culture invading the classroom. We’ve spent years turning normal human emotions into symptoms. Stress becomes a mental health issue," Alpert said, adding, "College should be one of the places where young people discover that they’re tougher than they think."

"A bad grade isn't psychological harm," Alpert continued. "Sometimes it's the wake-up call a student needs."

Fox News Digital reached out to the University of Michigan for comment.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

title: Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters
excerpt:
Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters a...
body_text:
Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea

The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships.

Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea.

Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers.

Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters.

This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November.

Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine.

The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel.

The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”.

The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025.

HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July.

Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm.

Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened.

“I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.”

title: DPD temporary workers may have missed out on sick pay and pensions, internal documents show
excerpt:
Missing payments suggest employment laws may have been breached by recruitment agencies used by courier company

Low-paid temporary workers at one of the UK’s top courier businesses have missed out on...
body_text:
Missing payments suggest employment laws may have been breached by recruitment agencies used by courier company

Low-paid temporary workers at one of the UK’s top courier businesses have missed out on entitlements to sick pay and pension contributions, internal documents suggest.

The payments – typically included in the “charge rate” that large brands pay recruitment companies to supply them with temporary workers – are missing from internal spreadsheets calculating the cost of employing thousands of transient staff working at DPD.

This absence suggests workers have either not been paid their entitlements, were discouraged from taking days off when sick, or were removed from roles before pension contributions became due, experts said.

Zoë Lagadec, principal at Mulberry’s employment law solicitors, said: “This raises questions if the workers are receiving statutory sick pay – as it doesn’t make sense that nobody gets ill – or if they are being moved on before 12 weeks service in order to avoid pension contributions.”

Withholding sick pay or pension contributions when they come due would be a breach of employment law by recruitment agencies and seemingly contravenes industry guidance published by the Association of Labour Providers.

The trade body’s charge rate guidance adds: “Supermarkets, brands and other labour users have a clear responsibility to ensure that labour providers throughout their supply chains are paid rates that fully reflect legal employment costs and compliance obligations.

“Labour users that pay unrealistically low rates are knowingly or recklessly conniving in illegality as these rates can only be achieved through worker exploitation, tax evasion or both.”

DPD promotes itself as “one of Europe’s leading parcel groups” and is wholly owned by France’s La Poste. It says its team exceeds 15,000 people, operating more than 10,000 vehicles from 84 locations and delivering more than 260m parcels a year. Its customers have included John Lewis, Marks & Spencer and Amazon.

The Guardian has seen internal DPD records detailing the discrete costs of more than 3,000 temporary workers hired by the courier during the past two financial years. The documents include hourly pay rates, holiday pay, employer’s national insurance contributions and a margin for the temporary recruitment agency, but do not include any sick pay or pension.

Industry experts questioned whether any temporary recruitment agency, which is technically the employer of the workers, could make any profit from DPD’s charge rates if it then paid the sick pay and pension entitlements to its thousands of staff.

Sick pay is now a right on the first day’s absence, although before April it only became due after three days off. Pension contributions are paid by the employer after 12 weeks in the job.

The Guardian outlined to DPD the records seen and what they appear to show. The company said: “Our commercial arrangements with our agencies allow them to fulfil their statutory obligations and are benchmarked against competitors in the industry.”

A spokesperson for the courier company added: “At DPD, we take our legal, regulatory and ethical responsibilities extremely seriously. As a client, engaging third-party employment agencies, DPD pays an agreed commercial charge rate to agency suppliers for providing temporary labour.

“Under UK employment law, recruitment agencies act as the primary employers of these agency workers. Consequently, statutory obligations, including the administration and payment of Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) and auto-enrolment pension contributions, sit directly with the agency suppliers, rather than DPD as the end-user client.

“Our contractual agreements require all agency partners to strictly follow all applicable employment legislation, including statutory pay and pension auto-enrolment requirements. We continuously review our procurement processes and supplier relationships to ensure our agency partners uphold the highest standards of compliance and fair treatment for all workers.”

The discovery of the data comes as the temporary recruitment industry looks at how the government’s new Fair Work Agency, which came into existence on 7 April, will use its powers to enforce workers’ rights.

The agency brings together much of the existing enforcement system into a single body, by combining the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority, the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate, HM Revenue and Customs’ national minimum wage enforcement unit and the Office of the Director of Labour Market Enforcement.

title: Hawaii contractor nominated to construct GOP comeback after two-decade Democratic hold on governor's mansion
excerpt: Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a k...
body_text:
Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a knife. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

Gary Cordery, who owns a contracting company, won the Republican nomination for Hawaii governor after defeating business owner Ken Fujiyama in Saturday's primary.

He is now set to face Democratic Gov. Josh Green in November in a race that heavily favors the incumbent. The Cook Political Report rates the contest as Solid Democratic, with a Partisan Voting Index of D+13.

Cordery faces a steep challenge: Hawaii has not had a Republican governor since Linda Lingle left office in 2010.

FORMER TOP OREGON GOP OFFICIAL SECURES NOMINATION FOR GOVERNOR AS REPUBLICANS TARGET BLUE-STATE PICKUP

Gary Cordery is running to become the next governor of Hawaii. (Gary Cordery for Governor via Facebook)

In addition to facing an incumbent with a 56% approval rating and Hawaii's long history of Democratic control, Cordery faces a significant financial disadvantage against Green.

Green has raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Cordery, who has raised about $313,000, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Despite the uphill battle, Cordery is pitching voters on a platform centered on lowering Hawaii’s high cost of living, reforming education and cracking down on corruption.

"As a husband, father and grandfather, businessman and community servant, I love Hawai’i," Cordery said in an interview with Honolulu Civil Beat. "These islands of unique beauty have endured mismanagement for decades. Her people live under tremendous stress and anxiety. I am running to open opportunity, create abundance and ensure stewardship of her resources, bringing accountability and hope for the people."

THE AMERICAN DREAM NOW COMES WITH A ZIP CODE: HERE'S WHERE STARTER HOMES ARE STILL WITHIN REACH

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green delivers remarks as President Joe Biden listens during a visit to an area devastated by wildfires in Lahaina, Hawaii, on Aug. 21, 2023. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

Part of Cordery's plan to create abundance includes adding 15,000 homes across the islands for working families, with prices ranging from roughly $400,000 to $600,000. His proposal calls for using state-owned land for fee-simple housing while streamlining permitting and opening more land for residential development.

An aerial view of the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina, Hawaii. (Kaanapali Alii Facebook)

He is also proposing eliminating the state's General Excise Tax on food and medicine and freezing property taxes for homeowners at retirement. Cordery argues that the state is failing to properly manage taxpayers' dollars and says he would order audits to root out waste.

"Hawai’i’s 20.5 billion dollar budget for 1.4 mil[lion] people is a staggering number. New Hampshire has 1.4 million people but a $7.75 billion dollar budget," Cordery said. "I believe our tax burden is out of control. The answer is management."

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Hawaii Gov. Josh Green cruises to Democratic primary win, sets up fall matchup with GOP nominee
excerpt: Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a k...
body_text:
Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a knife. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

Democratic Hawaii Gov. Josh Green defeated three little-known primary challengers seeking to lead the Aloha State.

Green, who was first elected governor in 2022, entered the unusual Saturday primary with a 56% approval rating. His primary win makes him a strong favorite for re-election, as the Cook Political Report rates the race 13 points in favor of the Democratic Party.

Green's opponents were David "Duke" Bourgoin, George "Teva" Lucas-Tadeo, a Democratic socialist, and Lauren Kapoliahiʻiaka Shim.

Bourgoin previously ran against Green for governor in 2022, but he captured only 590 votes compared with Green's 158,161. He also lost two bids for Honolulu mayor, in 2022 and 2024.

HAWAII'S DEMOCRATIC LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR INDICTED IN STATE CORRUPTION INVESTIGATION

Gov. Josh Green speaks onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2025 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 25, 2025, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for New York Hilton Midtown)

Despite the growing popularity of Democratic Socialists across the country, Lucas-Tadeo failed to win over Hawaii Democrats with public Instagram posts promising publicly run grocery stores and the legalization of marijuana.

Neither Lucas-Tadeo nor Shim had campaign websites, and none of Green's three challengers had raised any money in the race as of June 30, according to Honolulu Civil Beat. Meanwhile, Green had raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Republican Gary Cordery, the race's second-highest fundraiser, who had raised about $313,000, according to Civil Beat.

Hawaii has not had a Republican governor since Linda Lingle left office in 2010. In typical election years, the Democratic primary attracts candidates with strong name recognition. For instance, in 2022, the candidates besides Green included Rep. Kai Kahele, D-Hawaii, and former first lady Vicky Cayetano.

"His policies have been fairly popular, there hasn’t been anything he’s done that’s really created a pushback," John Hart, a communication professor at Hawaiʻi Pacific University, told Civil Beat. "So, why would you throw your hat in the ring on a suicide run when there are other offices that are more achievable?"

BABYLON BEE TOUTS LEGAL WIN OVER HAWAII GOVERNMENT'S 'WAR AGAINST POLITICAL MEMES AND SATIRE' IN FEDERAL COURT

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green delivers remarks as President Joe Biden listens during a visit to an area devastated by wildfires in Lahaina, Hawaii, on Aug. 21, 2023. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Green told Civil Beat that his administration responded effectively to the 2023 Lahaina wildfire, which killed 102 people, and flooding from the March Kona low storms, which caused more than $1 billion in damage.

Governor of Hawaii Josh Green, left center, points to damage as he speaks with FEMA Administrator Deanne Criswell during a tour of wildfire damage on Saturday, Aug. 12, 2023, in Lahaina, Hawaii. (AP Photo/Rick Bowmer)

"We were very present and I think pretty competent and compassionate in our response and we heard from a lot of people — both politicians and just, people — that they appreciated that," Green told Civil Beat.

"It just didn’t create a scenario in which another Democrat thought it made sense to run against us," Green continued. "I didn’t set out to get into fights with people, I really just tried to do this job. So, It didn’t create the usual opening where there was a big divide where people would come after me."

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Hawaii rep cruises to Dem primary win after challenger arrested for beach brawl
excerpt:

Progressive Rep. Jill Tokuda, D-Hawaii, cruised to victory in h...
body_text:
Police arrested Democratic congressional candidate Kirill Basin after he threatened individuals during a confrontation on a Maui beach.

Progressive Rep. Jill Tokuda, D-Hawaii, cruised to victory in her primary on Saturday, setting up a showdown with Republican state Sen. Brenton Awa in November.

Tokuda is seeking a third term representing Hawaii's 2nd Congressional District, which includes the entire state outside the island of Oahu, as well as rural and suburban parts of Oahu itself.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the district D+12. That means it's highly likely that Democrats keep hold of it in this year's midterms.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Rep. Jill Tokuda speaks as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve appear at a House Armed Services Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on May 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Tokuda defeated three primary challengers to win the Democratic Party nomination, though none posed a significant threat to her campaign despite a wider intraparty civil war that's toppled several House Democrat incumbents throughout the country.

Her fellow delegation member, Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, faced a significant primary challenge from his left in his own race, though Case is seen as much more moderate than Tokuda.

HAWAII DEMOCRATIC HOUSE CANDIDATE FACES FELONY THREAT CHARGES AFTER BEACH FIGHT CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, arrives for the start of the House Appropriations Committee markup of several appropriations bills in the Rayburn House Office Building on July 10, 2024. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Tokuda's race did attract some controversy, however, after one of her longshot opponents was arrested for a violent altercation that was caught on camera at Keawakapu Beach.

Kirill Basin allegedly threatened a man who asked him to turn down his music, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Video shows Kirill Basin swinging a beach chair during an Aug. 1 confrontation at Keawakapu Beach in South Kihei, Hawaii. (Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)

A violent clash ensued after a bystander intervened, and Basin allegedly pulled out a knife.

Tokuda told Hawaii News Now that the video was "disturbing" and said "any individual, whether you're running for office or a public citizen, you need to be held accountable for your actions."

title: Sydney gardener fined almost $200,000 for removing 287 trees to improve harbourside mansion’s water views
excerpt:
Local council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

It began with a gardener being hired to tr...
body_text:
Local council described incident as ‘worst act of environmental vandalism in Lane Cove history’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

It began with a gardener being hired to trim grass at a harbourside mansion in Sydney – and escalated to payments being left in a shoe for the unlawful felling of hundreds of native trees in protected bushland.

Now a court has fined Yi Wang $187,500 for his role in organising and carrying out the destruction of 287 trees from a council-owned foreshore bushland at Woodford Bay in Longueville in late 2023.

The New South Wales land and environment court justice Rachel Pepper convicted Wang last week for helping to orchestrate the clearing of 1,210 sq metres of land beside a waterfront property on Lucretia Avenue.

Wang pleaded guilty to three offences in relation to the unlawful clearing, which Pepper heard destroyed potential habitat for a range of protected and threatened animals, including powerful owls and microbats. It could take three decades to recover.

The unlawful tree clearing also greatly reduced the natural protection previously afforded to an Aboriginal midden, the court heard.

When it sold in 2014 for $7.6m, real estate agents described the Lucretia Avenue property as an “exclusive waterfront” residence commanding “water views from every room”. It boasted a private beach and was “bordering lush reserves”.

The director of Sydney Garden Home, Wang was hired by the stepdaughter of the owner of the adjacent property to the bushland, Yao Wu, for grass trimming work in November 2023.

The following day, Wu asked Wang to clear trees as well, including on public land.

“This is my back yard,” Wang would later claim Wu repeatedly told him.

Wang then hired casual labourers, including a chainsaw operator, and chopped down and removed trees over a 12-day period. The gardener sent regular updates on the progress of the work to his employer via WeChat and was paid in cash, which was often left in a shoe at the front of the adjacent property for Wang to collect.

Lane Cove council would later call those dozen days “the worst act of environmental vandalism” in the area’s history. The mayor, Scott Bennison, said the “outrageous” act needed to be “prosecuted to the full extent possible”.

In September 2024, the council installed a huge double-sided banner on the site of what it labelled “tree vandalism”, demonstrating its “commitment to obscure” harbour views gained by the destruction of the habitat and pledging it would remain in place until the trees grew back “to a suitable height”.

In addition to the fine and the publication of notices about the case in newspapers, Pepper ordered Wang to pay Lane Cove council’s legal costs.

In a statement, the council said it welcomed the judgment, describing it as “a win for native bushland”.

As it was awaiting the outcome of another matter before the court relating to the same location, the council declined to comment further.

The case first came to light through a tip-off from a member of the public. A council ranger then visited the site the day after the last day of clearing. Council officers discovered no approvals, permits, or consents had been issued for any tree removal and private investigators were engaged.

Recorded interviews from those investigators, as well as CCTV footage and invoices from a nearby dump, which showed Wang and the chainsaw operator disposing of ute loads of branches and vegetation, provided evidence for a timeline of events and facts that Wang did not dispute.

The council commissioned expert reports on the impact of the clearing, including by an arborist, a geologist and a senior archaeologist.

Wang argued his conduct was not reckless but rather negligent at its highest.

Pepper accepted references from his wife, mother and friend that Wang was otherwise a person of good character and was unlikely to reoffend.

The native forest canopy he helped clear had stood since at least 1943 and included an endangered ecological community.

Regeneration of the trees to a comparable ecological condition would probably take 20 to 30 years, a period during which regrowth would be susceptible to pathogens and weed invasion, the court heard.

title: Dem establishment strikes back as longtime incumbent fends off progressive challenger
excerpt: Democratic socialist Melat Kiros pulled off a primary upset against 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in Denver, signaling a far-left shift. Tom Del Beccaro weighs in on the Democratic Party's frac...
body_text:
Democratic socialist Melat Kiros pulled off a primary upset against 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in Denver, signaling a far-left shift. Tom Del Beccaro weighs in on the Democratic Party's fracture and further shift left.

The Democratic establishment won a key battle in the left's ongoing civil war with its socialist insurgency on Saturday.

Longtime Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, won his primary bid to seek another term in the House of Representatives, defeating progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole.

Case, who served in Congress from 2002 to 2007 and then won again in 2018, faced his toughest primary challenge yet this year. It comes amid a wider showdown between the Democratic establishment and its far-left flank that's seen multiple House incumbents lose to socialist upstarts.

SOCIALIST VICTORIES SHOW DEMS' DESCENT DOWN 'DEADLY PATH OF COMMUNISM,' JOHNSON WARNS

Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, arrives for the start of the House Appropriations Committee markup of several appropriations bills in the Rayburn House Office Building on Wednesday, July 10, 2024. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Keohokalole, who's been in Hawaii's state legislature since 2014, was the most formidable of a group of primary challengers looking to oust Case this year.

Both raised considerable money on the campaign trail, though the incumbent had more money in his war chest at the outset of the race.

Keohokalole criticized Case for not doing enough to stand up to the Trump administration during the president's second term, including President Donald Trump's federal immigration operations.

The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol on a hot and humid evening on Aug. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The progressive challenger also attacked Case for being one of four House Democrats to vote for Republicans' initial iteration of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act in April 2025.

JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN

That version would have imposed a federal voter ID requirement at the polls as well as a proof of citizenship mandate for registering to vote, but would have allowed for a written affidavit absent that proof.

Case told Hawaii News Now that he will "never" be someone who votes in lockstep with his party and said of the issue of noncitizen voting, "This has nothing to do with voter suppression. Now, those are fears and there are legitimate fears, and I accept those concerns."

"It’s a solution in search of a problem. There is no security problem in our election system," Keohokalole told the outlet.

Honolulu, on the south coast of the island of Oahu, is the capital of Hawaii and the gateway to this U.S. island chain in the Pacific. (Patrick Pleul/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Case later joined nearly all other House Democrats in opposing an updated version, the SAVE America Act, which would have vastly expanded the federal government's authority over state voter rolls.

He now goes on to face Republican Adriel Lam in November.

Hawaii's 1st Congressional District, which encompasses part of Oahu, including Honolulu, is rated a safe Democratic seat with a Cook Political Report rating of D+13.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Iran issues new demands as Pezeshkian seeks deal
excerpt:
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council has set out new conditions it says the United States must meet before the Strait of Hormuz can fully reopen.

Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of the counci...
body_text:
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council has set out new conditions it says the United States must meet before the Strait of Hormuz can fully reopen.

Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of the council, said on Saturday that the strait would remain closed until Washington “corrects its behaviour” in a statement published by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB.

The six conditions include an end to US threats against Iran and insults to what Zolghadr described as the country’s national and religious values; a permanent end to attacks against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq; the lifting of the US naval blockade and withdrawal of US naval and air forces from around Iran; compensation for damage from what he called two “imposed wars”; the lifting of sanctions; and the unconditional release of frozen Iranian assets.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) also said on Saturday that reopening Hormuz depended on Washington accepting the conditions and was separate from negotiations between Iran and Oman.

“Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened,” IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi was quoted as saying by the semiofficial Tasnim news agency.

The six conditions Zolghadr listed broaden the terms Iran now says must be met before Hormuz can reopen, tying the waterway to a more expansive set of political, military and economic demands than those set out in the June memorandum.

Most notably, they explicitly included Palestine, Yemen and Iraq alongside Lebanon in calling for an end to attacks against Iran and its allies. They also demanded an end to US threats and what Zolghadr described as insults to Iran’s national and religious values.

The conditions also call for the withdrawal of US naval and air forces from around Iran, full compensation for damage from what Zolghadr called two “imposed wars”, the lifting of sanctions and the unconditional release of frozen Iranian assets.

While some of these issues appeared in earlier proposals, the Reuters news agency reported that the June memorandum treated them as part of a reciprocal and phased process. Zolghadr is now presenting them as conditions Washington must meet before the strait can fully reopen.

That also differs from Washington’s latest position. An unnamed US official told Reuters on Friday that the blockade of Iranian ports would be lifted once commercial shipping through Hormuz was restored “without impediments”, with US steps tied to Iran carrying out its commitments.

Meanwhile, President Masoud Pezeshkian has backed efforts to reach an agreement, saying at a news conference with journalists broadcast by IRIB that he believed “now is the best time for an agreement”.

“There is cohesion, strength and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” he said.

Pezeshkian said Tehran and Washington should have established a mechanism for dealing with alleged violations of their earlier memorandum rather than allowing disputes to return to military confrontation.

“We need to see how to resolve them now, if a solution is possible, which is currently being worked on in the Oman negotiations,” he said, adding that he hoped Iran could move beyond the current state of “neither war nor peace”.

title: Trump’s White House ballroom foes face ‘very tough argument’ at Supreme Court, legal experts say
excerpt: Chanley Painter reports on the legal battle surrounding White House ballroom construction after an appeals court blocked the project. Former administration official Stephen Miller argues the facility ...
body_text:
Chanley Painter reports on the legal battle surrounding White House ballroom construction after an appeals court blocked the project. Former administration official Stephen Miller argues the facility is a national security necessity.

President Donald Trump could win the legal fight over his planned White House ballroom, say two legal experts who believe the U.S. the Supreme Court could end the case without weighing in on the underlying constitutional issue.

In a lengthy social media post Friday, Trump vowed to take the fight over his White House ballroom to the Supreme Court after the D.C. Circuit upheld a lower court order blocking above-ground construction. In a 2-1 decision, the appeals court ruled that the project cannot move forward without Congressional approval.

Trump pointed to the dissent written by Judge Neomi Rao, appointed by Trump in his first term, as grounds for appealing the decision to Supreme Court. Rao argued that the plantiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, lack legal standing in the case.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation built its case for legal standing around Alison Hoagland, a member who lives near the White House and regularly visits President’s Park. Hoagland said she visits the area about once a month and argued that the proposed ballroom’s size and design would diminish her enjoyment of the area by overshadowing the White House and weakening its aesthetic.

TRUMP SAYS WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM RULING JEOPARDIZES LIVES OF FUTURE PRESIDENTS, VOWS SUPREME COURT APPEAL

President Donald Trump has overseen ongoing construction of the underground military fortress that is going to be below the $400 million privately funded East Wing ballroom. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

But according to Rao, the National Trust did not establish the kind of injury necessary to invoke the courts’ authority to block the project.

"The district court elevated the aesthetic displeasure of a single passerby over the government’s security interests in the ballroom and the security risks of leaving an open construction site at the President’s home and office," Rao wrote.

Former Justice Department attorney Abhishek Kambli agreed, telling Fox News Digital the National Trust could face a particularly difficult hurdle on standing at the Supreme Court. He noted that, while Congress created the National Trust, the group still must show that its lawsuit is germaine to its interests.

"While they do have ownership of some properties, the President's Park, where the White House East Ballroom is, is not one of them," Kambli said. "And I think that's going to be a very tough argument to sustain, especially with the Supreme Court, that's more likely to agree with Rao than they are the [circuit court] majority, given the makeup of the Supreme Court, and the fact that the Supreme Court is very strict on standing."

OBAMA JUDGE RULES ON EFFORT TO BLOCK AMERICA 250 EVENTS AT WH AND LINCOLN MEMORIAL

President Donald Trump displays a rendering of his proposed $250 million White House ballroom as he meets with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 22, 2025. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Kambli also suggested that the National Trust faces a strong hurdle in proving it has standing based on aesthetic injury because it would have to prove it actually uses the space where the ballroom is being built

"Normally, aesthetic standing requires that you intend to use it," Kambli said. "So, for instance, if you're planning to be visiting the East Ballroom — and even this is kind of a stretch — that's one thing, but if you're someone on the outside that just passes it by, that's a little tougher."

A similar standing issue surfaced earlier in July when U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta, an Obama-appointed judge, rejected a lawsuit seeking to block the America 250 UFC event at the White House. He ruled that the plaintiffs had not met the standard of aesthetic harm to establish standing.

Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said he expects Trump to prevail on appeal as well, based on the standing issue.

"Under Supreme Court precedent, you cannot bring a claim, you cannot bring a lawsuit, until and unless you can demonstrate a concrete, actual injury," Spakovsky told Fox News Digital. "The idea that a passerby, who claims she will be aesthetically injured because of what she sees at the White House, has an actual injury is absurd, and obviously, and clearly defies that precedent."

If the Supreme Court takes the case, it could resolve it without deciding whether the administration had the legal authority to build the ballroom in the first place.

TRUMP WARNS JUDGE AGAINST SACRIFICING NATIONAL SECURITY BY BLOCKING WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM, DRONE BASE

President Donald Trump holds design for a proposed White House ballroom while speaking to reporters. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg)

"The Supreme Court won’t rule on the substantive issue if it can dismiss the case based on a lack of standing by the plaintiffs," von Spakovsky said. "I also don’t know of anyone else who could establish standing to bring a lawsuit. Perhaps Congress could collectively, but the chances of that happening are very slim given the partisan divides in both the House and Senate."

The National Trust argued in its lawsuit that federal law requires Congress to approve new construction on federal property in Washington, D.C., while the administration says existing law already gives the president authority to make alterations and improvements to federal property, including the White House.

Abhishek agreed with Rao’s reasoning that the terms "alteration" and "improvement" should be understood in their ordinary real-property sense.

"For instance, if I have an extension to my house, it doesn't become a new house," Abhishek said. "It's the same house, but that's an improvement done on the house. Or if I tear down some walls and then just create an open living space in my like between my living room and my kitchen, that's also not a new house at that point.

"It's the same house, but there was an alteration or an improvement done, so if you're using real property terms, then it's pretty clear how how the statutory authority would make sense," Abhishek continued.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Fauci in the congressional wringer: A test for Trump's newly-minted attorney general
excerpt:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on a Senate panel’s decision to refer Dr. Anthony Fauci to the Justice Department on ‘Special Report.’

Holding someone in contempt of C...
body_text:
Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on a Senate panel’s decision to refer Dr. Anthony Fauci to the Justice Department on ‘Special Report.’

Holding someone in contempt of Congress usually stems from them refusing to testify before a House or Senate committee or declining to provide documents and information requested by lawmakers. Especially if someone rejects an inquest by subpoena.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: WHY FAUCI'S 111 FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS COULD END UP BEFORE THE COURTS

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

You refuse to cough up the goods, and Congress may try to hold you in contempt.

And if you’re held in contempt, lawmakers may send a referral to the Justice Department. That’s kind of a parliamentary suggestion box, informing the feds that House Members or senators believe you’ve earned prosecution.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted recently to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress for refusing to answer questions at a hearing. The panel issued a subpoena to compel Fauci’s compliance. Republican senators say that’s all the more reason why Fauci should testify. They point to his pardon by then-President Joe Biden. That’s why they believe Fauci was obligated to answer their inquiries. Instead, he invoked the Fifth Amendment.

"On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution," said Fauci.

Twenty-one words. Uttered an astounding 111 times. That’s a grand total of 2,331 words. Fauci never deviated from the script.

WATCH: GOP SPLIT OVER RAND PAUL’S DOJ STRATEGY IN FAUCI CONTEMPT PUSH

"The goal was to wait for Dr. Fauci to make any kind of misstatement and then have a weaponized Department of Justice file criminal charges for that new statement that would not have been covered by the pardon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H.

So the panel took action. It voted 8-5 to hold Fauci in contempt. A party line vote.

"I've never voted to hold somebody in contempt. But if there's one person that should be held in contempt, it is Anthony Fauci," said Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla.

The Fauci conundrum could serve as a significant test for Attorney General Todd Blanche in his new role. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is the ranking Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security Committee.

He warned that the GOP gambit is dangerous.

"Criminal contempt is punitive. It does not compel a witness to answer questions or produce the documents we'd all like to see. What we'll do is create a damaging precedent that future witnesses will use to resist legitimate Congressional oversight and weaken this committee's ability to compel testimony."

Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., was unbowed.

"We will hand carry this over to the Attorney General. We will hand carry this to the district court here in (the District of) Columbia," said Paul.

Even though at the time, the DOJ only had an acting Attorney General.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

However, Paul was freelancing. He ignored the custom of the entire Senate voting to refer someone to the Justice Department for prosecution.

The Kentucky Republican himself previously sent other, unilateral referrals to the DoJ asking for Fauci’s prosecution. But those efforts never even went through committee. Fox can’t locate any precedent for such an independent maneuver. Especially circumventing the Senate floor.

Republicans control the Senate. It’s unclear whether there would be 51 votes to hold Fauci in contempt. But there is almost no scenario where the Senate could find 60 votes to break a filibuster on a contempt of Congress resolution of this nature.

This is why Democrats argued that Paul is out of line.

"No individual center senator and no committee speaks for the entire Senate as a whole," fumed Peters. "The chairman has also suggested he may attempt to refer this matter to the Department of Justice without approval of the full Senate. That would be even more dangerous and widely unprecedented."

Democrats argued that Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., was simply out of line. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The DOJ says it "seriously reviews all Congressional referrals." But Democrats believe the GOP’s disregard for Fauci invoking the Fifth could undermine any prosecution.

"It is almost certainly never going to be approved by a court because it violates basic constitutional rights," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.

In a statement, Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, accused Paul of trying to "weaponize the Justice Department" against his client. Democrats asserted that before Fauci’s hearing, Republicans cut them out of their inquiry.

"We have been excluded from witness interviews," said Peters.

FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS

But Republicans say Democrats showed no interest in their findings and revelations.

"They have all been uploaded on a website that you were invited to join," said Paul. "You never even asked for the password."

However, the Republican inquiry is just starting. Another Senate panel has now obtained a copy of the Health and Human Services phone Fauci used during the pandemic.

"It's frustrating we haven't gotten these devices until now. But now we have them," said Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., on Fox.

Johnson says decrypting that phone could answer questions which Fauci refused to address during the hearing.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted that "it's frustrating we haven't gotten these devices until now." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Two interesting developments emerged since Fauci testified in late July. First, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeannine Pirro dropped her prosecution of former Olympian David Hearn for allegedly vandalizing the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall. President Donald Trump then upbraided Pirro.

Does this mean that Pirro is doing things by the book? Would that diminish chances for prosecution of Fauci? Or, since Pirro enraged the president, could she redeem herself by prosecuting Fauci? After all, Trump said he wanted Fauci prosecuted.

However, the ultimate decision to prosecute is up to the new Attorney General, Todd Blanche. Sens. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Susan Collins, R-Maine, vowed to oppose Fauci. With former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., out, the GOP couldn’t lose any more votes without tanking the nomination. It boiled down to Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La. – who was undecided. Cassidy announced Friday morning he would vote yea on Blanche.

"I am particularly concerned about episodes of apparent lawfare. DoJ bringing suits against political enemies. Presidents of both parties have been guilty of this. It must stop. It should stop now. A never-ending cycle of prosecuting political enemies undermines the rule of law," said Cassidy. "I'm not entirely satisfied where where this is."

But Cassidy said he was comfortable enough to confirm Blanche.

Democrats will say any prosecution of Fauci is emblematic of the very weaponization which Cassidy fretted about. And this could be a special test case for the new Attorney General.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: James Carville responds to 'vicious' progressive Democrats trying to drive him out of the party
excerpt: Democratic strategist James Carville joins host Kayleigh McEnany to react to progressive Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed refusing to condemn controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker...
body_text:
Democratic strategist James Carville joins host Kayleigh McEnany to react to progressive Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed refusing to condemn controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

James Carville fired back at progressives who have suggested that the longtime Democrat leave the party, highlighting growing tensions between the moderate and progressive wings of the Democratic Party.

Speaking on "Saturday in America," Carville reacted to clips from Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's recent appearance on progressive influencer Hasan Piker's Twitch stream.

"James Carville fantasizing about leaving the party. I'm like, 'You're sweetening the deal,'" Piker said.

El-Sayed responded, "Why does anybody still listen to James Carville? He said one smart thing once, which he seems to have forgotten."

HASAN PIKER UNLOADS ON 'ISLAMOPHOBIC PIECES OF S---' DEMOCRATS AS EL-SAYED FACES PARTY UNITY TEST

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker appears on the campaign trail with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

Carville feigned distress, saying, "I don't know what I can do. I can't take it, please mama help me," before adding, "Such vicious people, wow."

El-Sayed, a progressive backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary Tuesday and will face Republican Mike Rogers in November.

Sanders defended El-Sayed and Piker on CNN, saying that if Carville doesn't want to share a party with progressives, "he can start his own party."

Carville responded by pointing to Sanders' status as an independent and past electoral defeats.

"When he was a socialist, I was a Democrat," Carville said. "I'm still a Democrat. Is he one now? I have no idea. I do know that maybe he has some animosity, because he tried twice to get the Democratic nomination for president, and he failed rather spectacularly both times."

BERNIE SANDERS TELLS JAMES CARVILLE TO START HIS OWN PARTY AS MODERATE DEMS WARN AGAINST 'EMBRACING EXTREMISM'

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed claps during a press conference in front of the Spirit of Detroit statue on Aug. 5, 2026, in Detroit. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Carville has repeatedly warned about the influence of progressives in the Democratic Party and previously told "The Sunday Briefing" that he would not remain in the party if far-left figures like Piker became a larger force.

JD VANCE WARNS 'LIMOUSINE SOCIALISTS' WILL DESTROY MICHIGAN AUTO JOBS, DEPRESS AMERICAN WAGES

"Look, I think that these, the progressive left, they're very tech people. I think they've come up with an AI random stupid idea generator," Carville said when asked about Francesca Hong, a progressive candidate for governor of Wisconsin.

"And I think the stupid idea generator can think of things that humans can't, like canceling Thanksgiving or being against interracial dating. So, I'm just waiting for the next stupid idea AI generator that comes out," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to Sanders, El-Sayed's campaign, Hong's campaign and Piker for comment.

James Carville attends The New York Times DealBook Summit 2025 at Jazz at Lincoln Center on Dec. 3, 2025, in New York City. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images for The New York Times)

Despite his concerns about progressives in the party, Carville said he thinks El-Sayed will win the Michigan Senate seat.

"[El-Sayed's] got some slack. He'd probably use every bit of it, but I still think he's going to win," Carville added.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

title: Graham replacement hopefuls make final pitches before special election: Iran war, DSA, Flock cams and more
excerpt:
'Fox & Friends' breaks down highlights from the South Carolina GOP Senate debate. Candidate Darline Graham pledges 100% support to Donald Trump's agenda and vows to nuke the filibuster.

Nine Republic...
body_text:
'Fox & Friends' breaks down highlights from the South Carolina GOP Senate debate. Candidate Darline Graham pledges 100% support to Donald Trump's agenda and vows to nuke the filibuster.

Nine Republican candidates vying to permanently fill late Sen. Lindsey Graham's Senate seat spoke directly to voters Saturday at an event in Florence County, South Carolina, where they addressed the war with Iran, the rising tide of socialism in the Democratic Party and potential privacy concerns around Flock cameras.

The event was hosted by Alan Wilson, South Carolina's Republican gubernatorial nominee, who pitched the gathering a kind of "speed dating," since each candidate was given six minutes to address the crowd.

The special Republican Senate primary is coming up on Aug. 11, which made Saturday's event one of the last chances for the candidates to make their closing arguments to voters.

Here's what they chose to focus on in their elevator pitches.

REPUBLICANS DEFY TRUMP, JUMP INTO SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE HIS HANDPICKED SUCCESSOR

Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., hugs his sister Darline Graham on stage as he announces his presidential campaign on June 1, 2015. (Jessica McGowan/Getty Images)

Sen. Darline Graham — who was chosen to finish out her brother's term after his death in July — was the last to speak but was quick to tell attendees that she intended to earn their votes.

"I'm not a politician. I never wanted to be a politician. But like Lindsey, I have a servant's heart. I am a hard worker. And yes, I have President Trump's endorsement, but I know I have to earn your votes," she said at the beginning of her speech.

She emphasized that she was not a "DEI" candidate, hyping her experience running the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, a state agency with a $90 million budget and dozens of employees.

"We help blind people and people with disabilities get jobs so that they don't have to rely on the government. How is that DEI?" she said.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., makes her way to votes in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN

She also made sure to highlight issues she and President Donald Trump agree on, including keeping transgender girls out of female sports, standing with Israel, supporting implementing voter ID through the SAVE Act and ending blanket birthright citizenship.

Graham briefly touched on socialism within the Democratic Party, calling it a problem that has to be stopped. She also described Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., as crazy.

Her speech concluded by answering a question about Flock cameras, which can automatically read license plates and are being installed all over the country.

"I need to look into that one, because there's two sides to that story. I know that some people are concerned about privacy and protecting their privacy, and I'm all for protecting the privacy of U.S. citizens. The other side of it is, if there's an emergency situation that an ambulance can be called quicker, and it can save lives," Graham said. "I'm going to be honest. That's a hard one for me. So I want to look into it a little bit more."

A Flock Safety camera is shown mounted to a light pole on August 3, 2026 in Beverly Hills, California. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., focused on his frustration with the Senate, calling it the place where "good bills go to die."

He proposed overhauling the Senate's rules to get measures like the SAVE Act passed.

"I will use my, whatever expertise I have to go to the Senate and force the vote, whether it's blowing up the filibuster or having a walking filibuster or getting with the parliamentarian and changing some of these stupid, arcane rules that the Senate has," Norman said.

The Senate filibuster allows a minority of senators to delay or block most legislation, effectively requiring 60 votes to advance a bill and making it harder for a narrow majority to enact its agenda.

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., speaks to reporters as he leaves a House Republican Conference meeting at the Cannon House Office Building on May 20, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED

Following his remarks, Norman was asked a question about the extent to which AI data centers should be regulated.

He said the federal government should not have a role but appeared to disagree with Trump's recent full-throated support of bringing data centers to communities around the country.

"Do I think it's bad for the community? Yes. Do I think it hurts the environment? Yes. And I will do whatever I can," Norman said.

An Amazon Web Services data center in Aldie, Virginia, on May 31, 2026. (Lexi Critchett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The key takeaway from former Myrtle Beach Mayor Mark McBride's speech is that he broke away from Trump's position on the war with Iran.

"Y'all, there is something we have to address if we're going to win in November," McBride said. "We need to end the war. We need to end the war now."

"We just have to admit we've lost the war. We've lost this battle," he continued. "Come home and regroup for another day."

He then addressed the crowd, saying: "There's not one of y'all in here who voted for President Trump a year and a half ago because this is where you thought we would be."

RETIRED LT. COL. RUNNING FOR CONGRESS BACKS TRUMP IRAN STRATEGY: 'HE'S ENDING A 47-YEAR CONFLICT'

Sam Shepherd, an engineer, inventor and entrepreneur, took the opposite approach to McBride, claiming he is "more conservative than Trump."

Shepherd cast himself as someone who has the skills to fix complex issues within the bureaucracy and the military.

He also took a moment to one-up Elon Musk, the former head of the Department of Government Efficiency, arguing he had more patents than the Tesla billionaire.

"I've actually authored more patents than Elon Musk. I have 44. I'm asking for you to bring common sense back to the government," Shepherd said.

Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., spent much of his speech tying the affordability issues Americans are facing to "onerous regulations."

"We see this on farms. We see this in every manner of our government — regulations strangle us," he said. "You've got to get government out of the way if we're going to solve this affordability crisis."

In response to a question about how he would secure the border if elected, Fry started off by attacking former President Joe Biden's work ethic and praising Trump's.

"You actually have to have a president who's awake for more than four hours a day, right? We went from a president who slept for 20 and was awake for four, to a president who is awake for 20 and sleeps for four," Fry said.

Fry said he would work to close "loopholes Biden used" to grant thousands of Haitians and Nicaraguans asylum in the U.S.

Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., speaks during the GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., on Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford zeroed in on the ballooning national debt, which is about to reach a staggering $40 trillion.

Sanford, who also twice served as South Carolina congressman, said the debt is incomprehensible and unsustainable.

"We've got a federal government that goes out and spends money it doesn't have, and then it turns around, and it prints money that's not there," Sanford said.

He argued that the growing national debt is inextricably linked to Americans reaching financial and life milestones later in life.

"The average age to buy a house, not that long ago, was 39 years of age, just 15 years ago. Today, that number is 59. In 15 years, it slid back 20 years, which is to say the American dream is becoming that much more difficult — whether it's my four boys or y'all's kids or grandkids out there," Sanford said.

Former Governor and Rep. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., speaks during the GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., on Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Mark Lynch, a businessman, was another candidate who favored getting rid of the filibuster.

He also said he wouldn’t "take a penny from AIPAC," making him one of the few candidates, along with McBride, to stake out a position at odds with the field’s staunch support for Israel.

Lynch's "number one" issue was his strong opposition to abortion. He talked at length about how he has spent time convincing women not to go through with terminating their pregnancies and how he has lobbied state legislators to toughen abortion restrictions.

Mark Lynch speaks during the GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., on Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Danny Ford II, the son of the championship-winning former head football coach at Clemson University, was the first to address Flock cameras and the potential privacy issues they raise.

He also talked about rapid data center development getting "out of control."

"It's getting pushed straight down our citizens' throats without any say so," he said.

On the issue of data centers, Ford said they need to be sustainable, produce their own power and not "leave a stain on South Carolina."

Glenda Gail Parker, a retired budget analyst with the U.S. Air Force, described herself as a conservative independent who leans Republican, but broke with Trump on energy policy, saying the country needs to reduce its reliance on fossil fuels.

In response to a question about how she would ensure South Carolina farmers get the assistance they need after natural disasters, Parker said she would work to mitigate "the climate extremes that we are experiencing now."

"And I do that by reducing our consumption of fossil fuels, and lower[ing] the demand for fossil fuels. In fact, today I want to challenge the oil and gas companies," Parker said. "Those companies that are interested in longevity must realize that they are in the energy business, not the oil and gas business. And so I would like to challenge the oil and gas businesses to clean up their image."

She concluded by saying the U.S. needs to pursue solar, wind, geothermal energy and hydropower.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Plastics contamination an ‘overlooked’ concern in food waste schemes, experts say
excerpt:
Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils

Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call on...
body_text:
Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils

Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call one of the most overlooked problems of the climate crisis, researchers have said.

This is despite the fact that, as the chef, author and activist Max La Manna puts it, food waste management is “one of the few climate problems where everyone wins”.

About one-third of all food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according to UN data. In the US, 40% of food waste goes to landfill, where it creates 30m metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent a year – more than Cuba’s total annual CO2 emissions in 2024, which amounted to 24.4m tonnes.

A new study, published in Nature Food, used life-cycle analysis modelling to compare the impacts – in terms of climate, nutrient pollution and plastic contamination – of different food-waste management scenarios.

The authors, based at the University of Vermont, compared the annual climate impacts of landfilled food waste with the climate impact of alternative recycling pathways and found that diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%.

These non-landfill scenarios could also reduce nutrient pollution in water bodies – a process called eutrophication that occurs when excess nutrients result in algal blooms.

But the researchers also said that microplastics can persist in compost, which could lead to 20,000 tonnes contaminating US agricultural soils each year. To date, no study has looked at the “plastic pollution footprint” of different food-waste management strategies at national scale.

Kate Porterfield, the lead author, said the method was comparable to working out a “carbon footprint of a product or process”. Essentially, the researchers looked at the process of managing food waste and “tall[ied] up what the carbon emissions are across all of those life-cycle stages”, she said.

Porterfield said the large proportion of wasted food still in packaging “goes bad before it even reaches the consumer”. One approach to recycling food waste is using a mechanical “depacker”; the packaging then goes to landfill, while food waste goes to “beneficial reuse, like composting or anaerobic digestion”.

However, they found that even if plastic separation technologies were 99% efficient, diverting food waste from landfill could still increase microplastic pollution in soil by an order of magnitude. “Any time where you’re diverting food waste, there is a risk of microplastic pollution” because “people aren’t perfect, machines aren’t perfect, and all of our food these days is packaged in plastic”.

The US state of Vermont has “one of the most ambitious” state organics-diversion mandates in the US, according to the co-author Eric Roy.

The state’s Universal Recycling Law has been fully effective from 2020 and requires food waste to be diverted from landfill. This applies to all households and means food scraps are banned from bins.

The authors said their findings provided an effective evaluation of the possible countrywide scale-up of such regulations and pointed to the need for “more attention to the plastics issue” from the outset of creating these policies.

Phil Holtam, a co-founder and director of the food waste social enterprise Sussex Surplus, said there was “a little bit of a misconception that [plastic packaging] is unnecessary”, and that it was a “necessary tradeoff”, essential to extending the shelf life of fresh produce, particularly for smallholder farms.

“That’s where the tension lies because as environmentalists we want to reduce food waste but we also want to prevent needless use of plastics.”

La Manna, who has worked with farmers in the UK and also witnessed food waste working in a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York, said consumer expectations of perfect-looking food were shaping what produce even made it to store shelves and adding to the waste problem. “Some of it may be misshapen, wonky, slightly cosmetically imperfect … [which is] challenging for supermarkets because they believe consumers want a perfect cucumber.

“We’re allowing ‘perfect’ to become this enemy of good.”

Roy underlined that in institutions such as schools, there “may be some well-intentioned rules that actually create challenges in moving away from highly packaged foods” because “food safety is always going to be a number one concern”.

Porterfield said that, ultimately, to reduce plastic contamination food waste management systems needed to be “as easy as possible to make it mindless for people to separate things efficiently”.

This included addressing the phenomenon of “wish recycling”, said Roy, where people put non-recyclable items in recycling in the hope they will be recycled.

He advised “old-school environmentalism” to reduce litter overall: “buy in bulk”, “make every effort to separate” – and “if in doubt, put it in the landfill stream”.

title: Perez Hilton faces long recovery after self-harm livestream
excerpt:
The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family.

Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members...
body_text:
The US blogger Perez Hilton is in a "serious but stable" condition after being admitted to hospital, according to his family.

Emergency services were called to his Miami home on Tuesday after members of the public reported concerns while watching a TikTok livestream.

The Miami sheriff's office confirmed they attended a scene of a man "livestreaming acts of self-harm" on Tuesday. They did not confirm his name but said the man was alone in the house at the time.

A statement released on the 48-year-old's website said he "experienced significant blood loss" and his treatment and recovery would be a "long process".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

The statement, external said Hilton was being held in hospital under Florida's Baker Act, which focuses on providing services for people experiencing a mental health crisis.

The father-of-three, whose real name is Mario Lavandeira, is expected to have surgery in the coming days.

A TikTok spokesman said its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream within minutes to the company's US moderation team for review.

A moderator error caused a delay in the removal, TikTok said, but the company alerted law enforcement to the situation, closed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds, and banned the account.

The pseudonym Perez Hilton is a reference to Paris Hilton who was at the height of her fame when the celebrity gossip blog was launched in 2005.

The website would go on to attract 8 million hits a day at a time when the internet was still in its relative infancy. It was criticised for vicious commentary of stars including Miley Cyrus and Lady Gaga.

In later years, Hilton admitted having regrets about being "mean or cruel".

He has also appeared on reality TV shows including Celebrity Rap Superstar and Celebrity Big Brother.
